course.title: Philosophy: Knowledge, Mind and Ethics
course.description: Test arguments row by row, meet Gettier and the sceptic, run a mind as a machine table and weigh lives behind the veil.
course.audience: An adult who has met validity and truth tables, as in Logic and Reasoning, and wants a rigorous university-style introduction to philosophy.

paragraphs: Look at a station clock that reads ten past three when it is ten past three, and believe the time it shows. Now suppose the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago. Your belief is true, and you formed it in the way that usually gives people the right time, and still it seems wrong to say that you knew it. Philosophy works with cases like this one, where an answer everyone has ready, about what knowing is, what a mind is or what we owe one another, meets a carefully built example and either survives or has to be repaired.

No telescope or survey will tell us whether a true belief counts as knowledge, or whether it can ever be right to harm one person to save five, and yet the answers decide how we weigh evidence and how we treat each other. Philosophy is the study of such questions, and it makes progress by giving reasons that other people can examine. Learning to read those reasons carefully lets you take a position on a hard question and say exactly why you hold it, and it lets you find the step at which someone else's argument, in a seminar or a newspaper, stops following.
outcomes: You'll be able to set an argument out in standard form and say which premise a speaker left unstated.
You'll be able to test whether a conclusion has to follow from its premises by looking for a counterexample.
You'll be able to explain why a Gettier case, a justified true belief that is true by luck, troubles the definition of knowledge.
You'll be able to say how dualism and physicalism differ and what the Chinese Room is meant to show about minds.
You'll be able to compare what a consequentialist, a Kantian and a virtue ethicist would each say about the same moral choice.
introduction.prerequisites: You should already know what a valid argument is and how to read a truth table, as covered in Logic and Reasoning.

lessons.title: Finding the argument

lead.text: The claim she wants you to accept is that we should eat early, and the film starting at seven and the restaurant being half an hour's walk away are offered as reasons for accepting it. Philosophers call statements arranged in this way an **argument**, and the word has nothing to do with quarrelling: an argument is a claim together with the reasons put forward for it. The claim being argued for is the **conclusion**, and each reason given for it is a **premise**.

Nothing in a sentence itself marks it as one or the other. “The film starts at seven” would be a conclusion if someone were defending it by pointing at the cinema's listings, and it is a premise only because here it is being used to support something else. What decides the matter is *the job a statement does* in the passage, so the question to ask of any statement is whether it is being argued for or being used to argue.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two passages in the figure. In the first, two premises work together, because neither the film time nor the walk gives much reason to hurry alone; in the second a single premise is enough. However many reasons there are, the test is the same: find the statement the speaker is trying to get you to accept, and everything offered in support of it is a premise.

model.passage: We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

conclusion.text: We should eat early.

model.passage: There will be no tables left: the queue already runs out of the door.

premises.text: The queue already runs out of the door.

conclusion.text: There will be no tables left.

lead.text: Your friend put her point first, but people just as often put it last or in the middle, so where a sentence stands can't tell us whether it is the conclusion.

What does tell us is a small word that speakers use to point the reasoning in a direction. “Because”, “since”, “after all” and “given that” sit next to a reason, while “so”, “therefore”, “hence” and “it follows that” sit next to a conclusion. We call them **indicator words**.

afterFigure.text: Indicator words are a guide, however, and *not a guarantee*. When the signposts are missing or ambiguous, fall back on the question from the last screen and ask which statement the others are there to support.

model.passage: The match will be called off, because the pitch is flooded.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

model.passage: Since the pitch is flooded, the match will be called off.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

model.passage: The pitch is flooded, so the match will be called off.

premises.text: The pitch is flooded.

conclusion.text: The match will be called off.

lead.text: Each premise goes on its own numbered line, a line is drawn beneath them, and the conclusion goes under it. This layout is called **standard form**, and it makes you settle everything that the original wording left loose.
To write a passage in standard form, take the indicator words out and let the layout do their work, since the line already means “so”. Then tidy each statement until it can *stand on its own*.

afterFigure.text: In both passages the conclusion ends up at the bottom, **under the line, where it follows from what is above it**. A good check on your reconstruction is to read it from the top as “this, and this, so that”, and see whether it still says what the speaker meant.

model.passage: We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.

premises.text: The roof still leaks.
New paint would be spoiled.

conclusion.text: We shouldn't repaint the hall yet.

model.passage: You will be late for the meeting: the 8:10 has been cancelled, and the next train arrives after it starts.

premises.text: The 8:10 train has been cancelled.
The next train arrives after the meeting starts.

conclusion.text: You will be late for the meeting.

lead.text: Standard form puts the conclusion last, but that is only a rule about layout.

The film starts at seven and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away, so we should eat early. Is that enough? It is only if we also take for granted that we want to be in our seats by seven and that dinner takes a good while, and neither was said, although without them the reasons would have nothing to do with the conclusion. People leave such things out because everyone present already accepts them, which means that a great deal of everyday reasoning contains a premise that is **unstated**: absent from the words, but needed for the reasoning to work. An argument with a gap of this kind is traditionally called an **enthymeme**, from a Greek word for something kept in the mind.

Supplying the missing premise is a careful job, because you may not add whatever helps the conclusion along. The premise should be one the speaker would accept, it should join the [[premises|The statements offered as reasons for a conclusion. Met in 'Finding the argument'.]] you were given to the conclusion, and it should claim no more than that join needs.

afterFigure.text: Dev's phone shows how much the wording matters. “Dev only switches his phone off when he is asleep” does the job, because it lets us go from the phone being off to Dev being asleep. “Dev's phone is off when he is asleep” sounds almost the same but would *not* do, since it says nothing about what else might switch the phone off.

model.passage: We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.
We want to be in our seats by seven.
Dinner takes a good while.

conclusion.text: We should eat early.

model.passage: Dev's phone is switched off, so he must be asleep.

premises.text: Dev's phone is switched off.
Dev only switches his phone off when he is asleep.

conclusion.text: Dev is asleep.

model.passage: Mira is a qualified pilot, so she holds a pilot's licence.

premises.text: Every qualified pilot holds a pilot's licence.
Mira is a qualified pilot.

conclusion.text: Mira holds a pilot's licence.

model.passage: The kettle is switched on at the wall, yet the water is cold after five minutes. So the kettle is broken.

premises.text: If the kettle is switched on at the wall and works, it heats the water.
The kettle is switched on at the wall.
The water is cold after five minutes.

conclusion.text: The kettle does not work.

lead.text: Take the film again: it starts at seven and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away, so we must leave the restaurant by half past six. Now suppose the reasoning goes on: a meal takes about an hour, so we should be sitting down by half past five. The claim about half past six, which was a conclusion a moment ago, is now being *used* as a premise.
A claim that is reached from earlier premises and then used to support a later claim is an **intermediate conclusion**, and the claim the whole argument is aimed at is the **final conclusion**.

afterFigure.text: To map a chain like this, find the final conclusion first, then ask what each of its premises rests on.

model.passage: The film starts at seven and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away, so we must leave the restaurant by half past six.

premises.text: The film starts at seven.
The restaurant is a half-hour walk away.

conclusion.text: We must leave the restaurant by half past six.

model.passage: We must leave by half past six. A meal takes about an hour, so we should be sitting down by half past five.

premises.text: We must leave the restaurant by half past six.
A meal takes about an hour.

conclusion.text: We should be sitting down by half past five.

blocks.text: Suppose a friend says, “We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.” Is she simply telling you three things she happens to know? She isn't, and you would hear that at once: one of the three is the point of what she said, and the other two are there to back it up.
Philosophy depends on being able to separate them, which is harder than it sounds when the reasons arrive in the middle of a paragraph, or when the most important one is never said at all.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to pick the conclusion and premises out of an ordinary passage, set them out in standard form, and say which premise a speaker left unstated.
intro.whyItMatters: Once an argument is laid out, you can ask of each premise whether you accept it.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is a conclusion together with the premises offered for it, and reconstructing one means asking what each statement is there to do.

blocks.text: To reconstruct an argument, find the **conclusion** first, as the statement the others are there to support, and use the indicator words as a guide without trusting them blindly. Then write the [[premises|The statements offered as reasons for a conclusion. Met in 'Finding the argument'.]] in **standard form**, supply any premise the speaker left *unstated*, and notice where one conclusion becomes a premise for the next.
What you end up with is the argument as it really stands, with nothing hidden in the phrasing, and that is the thing we can now test.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks the test question: given the premises, does the conclusion have to follow?

lessons.title: Valid, sound and counterexamples

lead.text: An argument is **valid** when it is impossible for all its [[premises|The statements offered as reasons for a conclusion. Met in 'Finding the argument'.]] to be true and its [[conclusion|The claim an argument is offered to support. Met in 'Finding the argument'.]] false, which is to say that if you grant the premises, the conclusion has no room to fail. Otherwise the argument is **invalid**, and any situation that makes every premise true and the conclusion false is a **counterexample** to it. One counterexample is therefore enough to show an argument invalid, while a valid argument has none.

Notice the word *impossible*. What matters is whether such a situation could arise, and not whether it ever has, so a counterexample can be as improbable as you like provided that it breaks no premise.

afterFigure.text: In the first we go from Ruth using the last of the milk to her buying more, and however hard you try you cannot make both premises true and the conclusion false. In the second we go from her buying more back to her having used the last, and now a counterexample is easy to find: **someone else used the last of the milk, and Ruth bought a carton anyway.**

cases.label: From using the last of the milk to buying more

model.passage: Ruth used the last of the milk yesterday, so she'll have bought some more.

premises.text: Whoever uses the last of the milk buys more.
Ruth used the last of the milk.

conclusion.text: Ruth bought more milk.

cases.label: From buying more back to using the last

model.passage: Ruth came in with a carton this afternoon, so she must be the one who used the last of it.

premises.text: Whoever uses the last of the milk buys more.
Ruth bought more milk.

conclusion.text: Ruth used the last of the milk.

lead.text: Hunting for a counterexample by imagining situations works, but it depends on how inventive you are, and failing to think of one *proves nothing*. For arguments built out of claims that are each either true or false there is a way that does not depend on imagination. In the pavement argument, “it rained overnight” and “the pavement is wet” are **atomic sentences**, meaning that neither has a smaller sentence inside it, and we can stand for them with the letters p and q. What is left when the atomic sentences are replaced by letters (“if p then q; p; so q”) is the argument's **form**.

Each atomic sentence is either true or false, so two of them can be combined in only four ways, and a list of all four ways, with the value of each premise and of the conclusion in each, is a **truth table**. A form is valid exactly when **no row has every premise true and the conclusion false**.

afterFigure.text: In the first, which reasons from rain to a wet pavement, no row makes both premises true and the conclusion false. In the second we reason from there being no rain to a dry pavement, and the row in which p is false and q is true is a counterexample: the [[conditional|An if-then claim, p → q. It is false only when p is true and q is false. Met in Logic and Reasoning.]] holds because its “if” part is false, “it did not rain” holds, and yet the pavement is wet.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It rained overnight.

conclusion.text: The pavement is wet.

cases.label: No rain, so a dry pavement

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It did not rain overnight.

conclusion.text: The pavement is not wet.

reveal.text: The two rows are p true with q true, and p false with q true. The first has a true conclusion, but in the second the conclusion p is false while both premises hold, and that row alone makes the form invalid. The lamp argument has the same form, which is why a lit room does not show that the lamp is plugged in.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
The pavement is wet.

conclusion.text: It rained overnight.

premises.text: If the lamp is plugged in, the room is lit.
The room is lit.

conclusion.text: The lamp is plugged in.

lead.text: “If p then q; p; so q” is **modus ponens**, from the Latin for a way of affirming, and it is valid whatever p and q stand for, so any argument of that shape is valid. “If p then q; q; so p” is **affirming the consequent**, which the last screen showed to be invalid, and it tempts us because it looks like modus ponens with the roles *swapped*. “p or q; not p; so q” is **disjunctive syllogism**, and the table confirms that it is valid.

afterFigure.text: Of the three, affirming the consequent is the one to be wary of, since arguments such as “if the engine is faulty the car won't start; it won't start; so the engine is faulty” have exactly its shape, and the car might equally have no petrol.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
It rained overnight.

conclusion.text: The pavement is wet.

premises.text: If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.
The pavement is wet.

conclusion.text: It rained overnight.

premises.text: The cat is in the garden or in the house.
The cat is not in the garden.

conclusion.text: The cat is in the house.

atoms.meaning: the cat is in the garden
the cat is in the house

lead.text: A new sentence can be true or false against every combination of the earlier ones, so **it doubles the rows**: two letters give 2 × 2 = 4, three give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, and four would give 16. Take “if the alarm rings, the guard wakes; if the guard wakes, the gate is locked; so if the alarm rings, the gate is locked”. It has three atomic sentences and so eight rows, and in none of them are both premises true while the conclusion is false, which makes the chain valid.

afterFigure.text: Reverse the conclusion, as the second view does, and the verdict changes. “If the gate is locked, the alarm rang” fails in the two rows where p is false and r is true (with q either true or false), because the premises say what follows from the alarm and nothing about what else might lock the gate.

premises.text: If the alarm rings, the guard wakes.
If the guard wakes, the gate is locked.

conclusion.text: If the alarm rings, the gate is locked.

premises.text: If the alarm rings, the guard wakes.
If the guard wakes, the gate is locked.

conclusion.text: If the gate is locked, the alarm rings.

lead.text: Two conditionals that end in the same claim q look as if they should link up, but they do not run into one another the way a chain does.

premises.text: If the alarm rings, the guard wakes.
If the gate is locked, the guard wakes.

conclusion.text: If the alarm rings, the gate is locked.

premises.text: If the kettle is on, the light is red.
If the toaster is on, the light is red.

conclusion.text: If the kettle is on, the toaster is on.

lead.text: So far we have asked only whether the conclusion would have to be true if the premises were, and that leaves half of the matter untouched, because validity does not say whether the premises actually are true. An argument that is valid and has only true premises is **sound**, and one that fails either test is **unsound**.

afterFigure.text: An invalid argument has failed at the first, since its conclusion does not follow, while a valid but unsound argument has a false premise, and its conclusion may then be true or false. Only a sound argument *guarantees* its conclusion.

premises.text: All mammals breathe air.
Whales are mammals.

conclusion.text: Whales breathe air.

premises.text: All cats are reptiles.
Whiskers is a cat.

conclusion.text: Whiskers is a reptile.

blocks.text: Here is an argument about a carton of milk: whoever uses the last of the milk buys more; Ruth has bought milk; so Ruth must be the one who used the last of it. Is there anything wrong with the argument?

Instead of asking whether the conclusion is true, we ask whether the premises leave any way for it to be false. Someone else might have used the last of the milk and bought more, and Ruth might have bought a carton for no reason at all, and then both premises would hold while the conclusion failed. Testing an argument comes down to a hunt for a case like that.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to test an argument for validity by looking for a counterexample, check a form with a truth table, and say whether a valid argument is also sound.
intro.whyItMatters: A valid argument can have a false conclusion, and an invalid one a true conclusion, so the test has to be about the link between them.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when no situation makes its premises true and its conclusion false, and it is sound when it is also valid with premises that really are true.

blocks.text: To test an argument, look for a **counterexample**: a way for every premise to be true while the conclusion is false. For a form built from atomic sentences a truth table searches every row for you, and it grows by a factor of two with each new sentence. Finding one such row shows the argument is *invalid*, and finding none shows it is valid.

Validity concerns only the link between premises and conclusion, so a second question remains, whether the premises are true. An argument that passes both is **sound**, and that is the kind that gives you a reason to believe its conclusion.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to arguments that look better than they are, and to what fairness requires when you answer someone else's.

lessons.title: Fallacies and charity

lead.text: A pattern of reasoning that looks as though it supports its conclusion, but does not, is called a **fallacy**. The ones we meet now are called *informal*, because you find them by looking at what an argument does with its content and not by building a table.

The simplest is to reject a claim by attacking the person who makes it instead of the reasons they give. Take Jo, who has proposed one meat-free day a week in the school canteen, and a neighbour who answers, “Jo's a vegetarian, so ignore her.” Laid out as an argument, that reply rests on an [[unstated premise|A premise the speaker leaves out because they expect you to supply it. Met in 'Finding the argument'.]]: that nothing a vegetarian says about school meals deserves attention. This move is called **ad hominem**, Latin for “to the person”.

afterFigure.text: Facts about a speaker can matter, since a reviewer who is paid by the seller gives us a reason to check what she says more carefully. The fallacy lies in treating such a fact as though *it settled the question*, so that the argument itself is never examined.

model.passage: Jo's a vegetarian, so ignore her.

premises.text: Jo is a vegetarian.
Nothing a vegetarian says about school meals deserves attention.

conclusion.text: Jo's suggestion can be ignored.

model.passage: Ignore her review of the phone, since she works in the shop.

premises.text: She works in the phone shop.
Nothing a shop worker says about a phone deserves attention.

conclusion.text: Her review of the phone can be ignored.

lead.text: A reply that begins “So Jo wants to stop our children eating meat” sets up a much bolder claim, one that is easy to knock down, and then knocks it down, so that Jo's own proposal is never touched. This is the **straw man**: a flimsy figure put up in place of the real opponent and defeated because it is flimsy.

afterFigure.text: The straw man lands on a claim nobody made, while the fair reply, “one day a week is too few to change what children choose to eat”, lands on the claim that was made and so *can be judged on its merits*. A useful test is to ask whether the person you are answering would say, “yes, that is what I meant.”

lead.text: Consider: “Nothing is better than a day at the beach. A cold, wet Monday is better than nothing. So a cold, wet Monday is better than a day at the beach.” Each premise is true on a sensible reading and the conclusion is plainly false, so something has gone wrong, and what has gone wrong is the word “nothing”. In the first premise it means that no activity at all beats the beach, while in the second it means an empty day on which nothing happens. Using a word in more than one sense within one argument is **equivocation**.

afterFigure.text: The argument is really two arguments joined by a word that sounds the same. To catch equivocation, take each key word and ask whether it means the same each time it appears; when it does not, the connection between the premises has been *lost*.

lead.text: Two further failures concern the support itself. “Parking in the town centre should be free, because it ought not to cost anything to park there”: the reason says the same thing as the conclusion in other words, and so gives no one a reason who did not already accept it. An argument whose premise assumes its own conclusion is **begging the question**, or circular.

In the second, the support is real but the choices have been rigged. “Either we serve chips every day or the children go hungry.” If those were the only two options, the case for chips would be strong, but they are not, and an either-or that leaves out options which exist is a **false dilemma**.

afterFigure.text: To test for circularity, ask whether someone who doubted the conclusion could accept the premise without already having accepted the conclusion. To test an either-or, count the options offered and then ask whether any more exist.

lead.text: When someone says, “Children aren't eating enough vegetables, so the canteen should serve more,” there is an [[unstated premise|A premise the speaker leaves out because they expect you to supply it. Met in 'Finding the argument'.]] to supply, and you have a choice. You could supply “Schools should force children to eat vegetables”, which is easy to attack and which the speaker probably doesn't believe, or you could supply “A school canteen should make it easier for children to eat what they are short of”, which a thoughtful speaker would accept. The **principle of charity** tells you to choose the second: reconstruct an argument in the strongest form that fits what was *actually* said, and only then assess it.

afterFigure.text: It doesn't mean agreeing, because the strongest version of an argument can still fail, and it doesn't mean adding more than the argument needs, since a premise stronger than the speaker's reasoning requires makes it a new argument. Nor is it kindness for its own sake, because **a criticism of the strongest version is the only kind that counts against the view**, while defeating a weak version tells you only that the weak version was weak.

blocks.text: “Ignore her review of the phone,” someone says, “since she works in the shop.” She does work in the shop, so she may have reason to talk the phone up, which is worth bearing in mind; but whether the phone is any good depends on the phone, and the reviewer's job doesn't settle that.

A name lets you say exactly what has gone wrong instead of only that something has. There is a second skill that matters at least as much, which is answering an argument in its strongest form. Before you criticise an argument you need to ask what the best version of it would be.

recap.keyIdea: A fallacy is reasoning that only looks like support, and the principle of charity says to answer the strongest version of an argument, not the weakest.

blocks.text: Five informal fallacies cover a great deal of bad argument: **ad hominem** attacks the speaker, a **straw man** attacks a position nobody took, **equivocation** changes a word's meaning midway, **begging the question** assumes its conclusion, and a **false dilemma** hides options. Each can be caught by asking one question about what the argument is actually doing.

The *principle of charity* turns the same care on your own reply: supply the [[unstated premise|A premise the speaker leaves out because they expect you to supply it. Met in 'Finding the argument'.]] a thoughtful speaker would accept, restate the position fairly, and only then decide whether it holds.

lessons.title: Knowledge and Gettier cases

lead.text: Look again at the two people at the coin. Both believe it landed heads, so belief is not what separates them, and both are right, so neither is truth. What the watcher has is a reason, her evidence from seeing the coin land, and the guesser has none. That suggests an answer: to know something is to have a belief that is true and that you hold with good reason. The proposal is called the **justified true belief** analysis, and it is traditionally traced to Plato, whose Socrates considers a close relative of it, true belief together with an account of why it is true, in the *Theaetetus*.

The analysis builds knowledge out of three conditions, all of which have to be met. You must *believe* the claim, the claim must be *true*, and your belief must be **justified**, meaning supported by good reason or evidence and not held on a hunch.

afterFigure.text: In the figure Kofi, who watched the coin, meets all three conditions, while Tess meets the first two but not the third. The conditions are checked separately, and failing one is enough to withhold knowledge, which is why Tess does not know although she turned out to be right.

lead.text: Each condition can fail on its own.

For a long time the analysis seemed to need no repair, and then in 1963 Edmund Gettier published a paper of only three pages, “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?”, in the journal *Analysis*. It describes cases in which someone has **a justified true belief and, it seems, does not know**.

Smith and Jones have both applied for the same job. The company president has told Smith that Jones will get it, and Smith has counted the coins in Jones's pocket and found ten. He therefore has strong evidence for the claim that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, and from it he infers that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Now suppose that the president was wrong. Smith himself gets the job, and, without knowing it, he too has ten coins in his pocket.

model.fact: Smith gets the job, and Smith happens to have ten coins in his own pocket.

lead.text: Smith's belief meets all three conditions. He believes it, it is true, since the man who gets the job does have ten coins, and it is justified, because he reasoned carefully from strong evidence. On the analysis, then, Smith knows. Yet it is hard to say that he does. His belief is true, but not for the reason he had: his evidence was about Jones's job and Jones's coins, and it is facts about *himself* that he knew nothing of that make the belief true. His evidence and the truth have come apart, and the fact that they land on the same claim is luck. A case of this kind, where someone has a justified true belief but seems not to know because it is true by luck, is called a **Gettier case**.

afterFigure.text: Kofi's evidence is connected to the fact that makes his belief true, because he watched the coin land, while Smith's evidence has no connection to the fact that makes his belief true. Both meet the same three conditions, and so the analysis cannot tell them apart. If they differ, as they seem to, **then justified true belief cannot be the whole story about knowledge**.

steps.headline: Ravi sees rain: the analysis applied to a case that works

workedSteps.text: Ravi looks out of the window and sees rain falling on the street, and he believes it is raining outside. He does believe it, so the first condition is met, and it is raining, so the belief is true.
For justification we ask what he has to go on. He is watching the rain fall, which is about as good a reason as anyone could have, so the belief is justified.
Ravi meets the same three conditions that Smith did, and yet nobody hesitates to say that Ravi knows. Ask yourself what is different about his case.
The difference is that Ravi's reason is the very fact that makes his belief true. The analysis gives the right verdict for him, and the trouble lies in cases where reason and fact come apart.

reveal.text: Bertrand Russell described a case of this kind in 1948, some years before Gettier's paper, so the idea that true belief can be right by accident was not new in 1963.

workedSteps.text: Ana looks at the station clock, which is usually reliable, and sees that it reads 2:15. She comes to believe that it is 2:15, so the first condition is met, and a clock that is usually reliable gives her good grounds, so the belief is justified.
It is in fact 2:15, so the belief is true, although the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago and she has looked at it at the one moment of the day when it is right.
Now apply the analysis to the case. Does it say that Ana knows the time?

lead.text: A condition is **necessary** for something if the thing cannot happen without it, and **sufficient** if having it guarantees the thing. Having four sides is necessary for being a square, since a square without them is impossible, but it is not sufficient, because a rectangle has four sides without being a square.

In his cases the person meets all of them, so nothing he said stops belief, truth and justification from being *necessary* for knowledge. What his cases show instead is that **having all three does not guarantee knowledge**, so something more is needed.

Smith's reasoning ran from “Jones will get the job”, which is false, to a conclusion that happened to be true. A step along the way in an argument is a lemma, so the pattern suggests a repair: add a fourth condition, that **no false lemmas** may figure in the reasoning by which you reach your belief.

Smith has strong evidence that Jones owns a Ford, since Jones has always owned one and has just offered him a ride in it. Picking a place at random, Smith infers “Either Jones owns a Ford or Brown is in Barcelona”, which holds as soon as either half does. Jones in fact rents the car, but by sheer chance Brown is in Barcelona, so the belief is true and Smith's reasoning once more passed through something false.

afterFigure.text: Both are repaired by the new condition, but only because a false step *happened* to be present.

lead.text: Henry is driving through a county in which, unknown to him, most of the barns by the road are facades built to look like barns from the road. He looks at a building in good light and believes “that is a barn”, and by luck it is the one real barn in the county. Henry's reasoning contains no false step at all, since he reasoned from how the building looked, and yet he doesn't seem to know.

Think back to Ana and the stopped clock. Her belief could very *easily* have been false, because had she looked at the clock a minute earlier or later she would have believed that it was 2:15 and been mistaken. A belief that could not easily have been false, in the sense that it would be true in any nearby situation in which you formed it in the same way, is a **safe belief**. Kofi's belief, formed by watching the coin, is safe, while Ana's is not, and a repair that asks for safety therefore rules her out. You can put the same test to Henry, by asking what he would have believed had he looked at a different building on that road.

afterFigure.text: Neither repair has won general agreement.

blocks.text: Two people say that the coin landed heads. One of them stood beside it and watched it land. The other called heads before it was tossed, for no reason at all, and turned out to be right. Both believe that it landed heads, and both are correct, yet we wouldn't say that the second one knew. What does the first have that the second lacks?

For a very long time philosophers gave the answer that looks obvious: the first has a good reason and the second has not. That answer can be tested until it breaks, and the cases that break it are surprising, because in them the person has a true belief and a good reason for it and still seems not to know.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to apply the three conditions for knowledge to a case, explain how a Gettier case defeats them, and say what the no-false-lemmas and safety repairs add.
intro.whyItMatters: Whether you know something, and not merely believe it correctly, decides what you should rely on.

recap.keyIdea: Knowledge was long taken to be justified true belief, but Gettier cases meet all three conditions by luck, so the three are not sufficient.

blocks.text: On the traditional analysis, knowing is having a belief that is **true** and **justified**. Gettier cases, such as Smith and the ten coins, meet all three conditions while the truth of the belief is a matter of luck, which shows that the conditions are necessary but *not sufficient*.

Two repairs have been tried: that the reasoning must contain no false lemmas, and that the belief must be safe from easy error. The second covers cases, such as the fake barns, that the first misses, but neither has settled the question.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks a harsher question: whether we can know much of anything at all.

lessons.title: Dreams, demons and closure

lead.text: In the First Meditation, published in 1641, René Descartes looks for a belief that no reasoning could undermine. The senses sometimes deceive us, but only about things that are small or far away, he thinks, so he cannot doubt that he is sitting by the fire in his dressing gown, holding a piece of paper. Then he remembers that he has often dreamed that very thing, and that nothing he can name, neither the vividness nor the detail, reliably separates being awake from being asleep.

Whether he is awake or dreaming, Descartes notes, two and three still add up to five and a square still has four sides. What it undermines is our confidence in beliefs about the world around us, which depend on the senses.

afterFigure.text: It does not say that you *are* dreaming, only that **you cannot tell from the inside that you are not**, and that this seems to be enough to take your knowledge of your surroundings away.

lead.text: Suppose, he says, that the source of my beliefs is not a good God but some malicious demon of the utmost power and cunning, who has devoted all his effort to deceiving me. A scenario of this kind, in which everything would seem to you just as it does now and yet your beliefs would be systematically wrong, is a **sceptical hypothesis**, and the dream and the demon are the first two.
However thoroughly the deceiver misleads him, there has to be someone who is being misled, and so “I exist” is true whenever he thinks it.

afterFigure.text: The hypothesis has since been given a modern costume, in which you are a brain kept alive in a vat by scientists who feed it experiences by computer.

lead.text: A sceptical hypothesis would not matter if it only concerned remote possibilities, so how does the sceptic get from it to a claim about what you know? Having hands entails that you are not a handless brain in a vat, or in Descartes's version, that you are not being deceived by a demon. So if you know that you have hands, and you know this entailment, you ought to be able to work out that you are not deceived. The principle behind that thought is called **closure**: if you know p, and you know that p entails q, then you know q.

Now add what the sceptic wants us to grant, which is that you do *not* know that you are not being deceived, since every experience you could cite would be the same if you were. With closure, the sceptic concludes that you do not know you have hands either.

afterFigure.text: If it holds, the sceptic's second premise is enough to take away knowledge of the ordinary world, and so the question is whether the argument is valid, which we can settle, and whether its premises are true, which is the real dispute.

lead.text: The sceptic's argument has the form “if p then q; not q; so not p”, which is called **modus tollens**, Latin for the way that denies. It is valid, as a [[truth table|A list of every way the sentences could be true or false, with the verdict in each. Met in 'Valid, sound and counterexamples'.]] shows: in every row that keeps both premises true, the conclusion “not p” is true as well.

It is easy to confuse with two forms that have no such guarantee. Denying the first part (“if p then q; not p; so not q”) and affirming the second (“if p then q; q; so p”) each have a [[counterexample|A situation in which every premise is true and the conclusion false. Met in 'Valid, sound and counterexamples'.]]: in both, the row with p false and q true keeps the premises true and the conclusion false.

afterFigure.text: Only modus tollens does the sceptic's job, because it alone works backwards from the denial of the second half to the denial of the first.

lead.text: In 1939 G. E. Moore gave a lecture, “Proof of an External World”, in which he held up his hands and said, “Here is one hand, and here is another.” He is more certain that he has hands than he could be of any philosophical premise, and so he keeps the sceptic's first premise and adds that he knows he has hands. By [[modus ponens|From “if p then q” and p, infer q. Met in 'Valid, sound and counterexamples'.]], it follows that he knows he is not being deceived.

Both share the conditional premise and differ in the second one, since the sceptic *denies* that we know we are not deceived and Moore *affirms* that we know we have hands. Each rules out the other's conclusion, and **neither can win on logic**.

afterFigure.text: The disagreement is now entirely about which premise is more credible, and critics of Moore object that his argument seems to give us knowledge that we are not deceived, a conclusion that no experience could ever confirm.

steps.headline: Two valid arguments from one conditional premise

workedSteps.text: Both arguments share the conditional premise: if I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived by a demon. Call the two halves p and q.
The sceptic adds not-q, since nothing in my experience could show I am not deceived, and concludes not-p by modus tollens.
Moore adds p, since he is sure he has hands, and concludes q, running the shared conditional forwards. The arguments contradict each other, and yet each is valid. How can that be?
Neither argument can be faulted on its form, so the choice is between their second premises, and that choice is a matter of which one is more believable.
Moore accepts the shared premise: if I know I have hands (p), I know I am not deceived by a demon (q).
He then affirms the first half: I know I have hands. So he holds both p → q and p.
From these two premises he reaches q, that he knows he is not deceived. Name the rule that takes p → q and p to q.

lead.text: The other way to answer the sceptic is to reject the first premise, the claim that if you know you have hands, you know you are not deceived. In his paper “Epistemic Operators” (1970), Fred Dretske asked about someone at the zoo who knows that the animal in the pen is a zebra. Does she thereby know that it is not a mule cleverly painted to look like a zebra? Dretske thought she doesn't, since nothing she has could tell the two apart, and yet being a zebra entails not being a disguised mule.

Robert Nozick, in *Philosophical Explanations* (1981), reached the same place by a different route. He said that you know p only if your belief *tracks* the truth, so that if p were false you would not believe it. If you had no hands you would not believe that you did, so you know you have hands. If you were a handless brain in a vat you would still believe that you were not, so you do not know that you aren't. Both philosophers can therefore say that **we know ordinary things and still lack knowledge of the sceptic's denial**.

afterFigure.text: The price is that the principle behind that premise is intuitive. Saying “I know I have hands, but I don't know I'm not a handless brain in a vat” sounds odd even to those who defend it, and critics think that oddness counts against the reply.

blocks.text: How do you know that you aren't dreaming right now? If nothing you can point to separates the two cases, do you really know that you are awake and reading this?

Philosophers take the question seriously because the same worry reaches almost everything we claim to know about the world, and it can be set out as a short argument whose conclusion is that you don't know you have hands. Once the argument is laid out, the question becomes an exact one: which premise should we give up, and what does each choice cost us?

blocks.text: The sceptic argues from a **sceptical hypothesis**, such as Descartes's demon, together with *closure*: if you know you have hands you would know you are not deceived, and you don't know that, so you don't know you have hands. The form is modus tollens and it is valid, so a reply has to reject a premise.

Moore keeps closure and affirms that he knows he has hands, running the same argument forwards by modus ponens. Dretske and Nozick instead give up closure, accepting that we can know ordinary things without knowing that the sceptical hypothesis is false.

lessons.title: Evidence and credence

lead.text: Take a town of 1,000 people in which 200 have a particular condition, and a test for it. One is the share of people with the condition whom it flags, here 60%, which is called the **hit rate**, and the other is the share of people without the condition whom it flags anyway, here 5%, which is called the **false alarm rate**.

Of the 200 people with the condition the test flags 60%, which is 120. Of the 800 without it, it flags 5%, which is 40. Everyone flagged is in one of those two groups, so the test flags 120 + 40 = 160 people in all.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws the town as a grid and lets you compare this test with a sharper one that raises fewer false alarms. Notice that the hit rate is a fact about the 200 people with the condition and the false alarm rate is a fact about the 800 without it, so the two rates apply to groups of very different sizes.

lead.text: Go back to the town of 1,000 people at the start of the lesson, where the test flagged 160 people. Of those 160, 120 have the condition, which is 120 ÷ 160 = 75%. Philosophers who study how evidence should change belief call a degree of belief, written as a number from 0 (certainly false) to 1 (certainly true), a **credence**. Your credence before the test is the **prior**, here 200 in 1,000, or 0.2, and your credence after it is the **posterior**, here 0.75.
Among all the cases that fit the evidence, ask what share also fit the hypothesis, and let that share be your new credence.
A positive result raised the credence from 0.2 to 0.75 without making it *certain*, which is what we should expect from evidence that is good but not perfect.
The prior is the credence you hold before the evidence arrives.

steps.headline: From the rates to the posterior, step by step

workedSteps.text: Take 1,000 people, 200 of whom have a condition. The test has a hit rate of 80% and a false alarm rate of 5%. Start with the people who have the condition: 80% of 200 is 160, so 160 of them test positive.
Now the people without the condition. There are 800 of them, and 5% of 800 is 40, so 40 of them test positive as well.
In all 160 + 40 = 200 people test positive, and the posterior is the share of them who have the condition. Why do we divide by 200 and not by 160?
The share is 160 ÷ 200 = 80%, so someone who tests positive has a posterior of 0.8, up from a prior of 0.2.

lead.text: Whether a positive result should alarm you depends on how common the condition was to begin with. How common it is in the group you belong to is called the **base rate**. Suppose the condition affects only 2% of people, and the test has a hit rate of 90% and a false alarm rate of 5%. Of 1,000 people, 20 have it and 18 of them test positive, while 980 do not and 49 of them test positive. The test flags 18 + 49 = 67 people, of whom only 18 have the condition, which is about 27%.

Few people expect that, because a test with a 90% hit rate sounds as if a positive result should settle the matter. The error of judging by the hit rate while ignoring the base rate is called **base-rate neglect**, and psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky documented it in experiments in the 1970s.

afterFigure.text: Switch to the figure's second case, where the condition affects 20% of people. There 180 of the 200 with it test positive against 40 of the 800 without it, so about 82% of the positives have the condition. The test has *not changed at all*, only the base rate, and that single change moves the posterior from about 27% to about 82%.

steps.headline: A rarer condition, counted in full

reveal.text: Of those 108 positives only 9 have the condition, so the posterior is 9 ÷ 108, or about 8%. A positive result from this test raises a credence of 1% to only about 8%, because the 990 healthy people produce far more false alarms than the 10 ill people produce hits.

workedSteps.text: Now only 1% of 1,000 people have the condition, which is 10 people, and the test has a hit rate of 90% and a false alarm rate of 10%. Of the 10, 90% test positive, which is 9 people.
Of the 990 without the condition, 10% test positive, which is 99 people.
Add the two groups to find how many people test positive in all.

lead.text: The **odds** of a hypothesis compare the cases in which it is true with those in which it is false, so a prior of 10% corresponds to odds of 1 to 9. The strength of a piece of evidence can be summed up in one number, the **likelihood ratio**, which is the hit rate divided by the false alarm rate. For a hit rate of 90% and a false alarm rate of 10% it is 0.9 ÷ 0.1 = 9.

To update, multiply the prior odds by the likelihood ratio, and the result is the posterior odds. With odds of 1 to 9 and a ratio of 9, the posterior odds are 9 to 9, or 1 to 1, which is a probability of one half. The same test applied to a 1% prior, with odds of 1 to 99, gives 9 to 99, which is the 9 in 108 we counted a moment ago.

afterFigure.text: The practical lesson is that the likelihood ratio belongs to the *test* and not to the *person* tested.

lead.text: Write P(H) for the probability of the hypothesis, P(E | H) for the probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is true, and P(H | E) for the probability of the hypothesis once the evidence is in. **Bayes' theorem** says that P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) ÷ P(E), where P(E) is the probability of the evidence overall, that is, P(E | H) × P(H) added to P(E | not-H) × P(not-H).

Read with our numbers, the top is the share of people who both have the condition and test positive, and the bottom is the share who test positive at all. For the 10% case that is 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.09 on top, and 0.09 + 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.18 on the bottom, so the posterior is 0.09 ÷ 0.18 = 0.5, as before.

afterFigure.text: The formula adds *no new idea* to the counting.

blocks.text: A screening test is positive for 90% of the people who have a condition, and also, by mistake, for 10% of the people who do not. Yours comes back positive. How likely is it that you have the condition? Most people say about 90%, and it feels like the obvious reading of the numbers.

It is not, because the answer depends on a number that the question never mentioned, which is how common the condition is. The more useful question is how strongly to believe something given the evidence, and there is a precise way to answer it.

recap.keyIdea: Evidence should change your credence by an amount that depends on the prior, the hit rate and the false alarm rate together, and never on the hit rate alone.

blocks.text: To update a **credence**, start with the prior, count how many cases with and without the hypothesis the evidence would flag, and take the share of the flagged cases that fit the hypothesis. The same result can be reached by multiplying the prior odds by the *likelihood ratio*, or by Bayes' theorem.
The hit rate on its own never decides the answer: when the **base rate** is low, even a good test produces mostly false alarms, and ignoring this is base-rate neglect.

lessons.title: Mind and body

lead.text: Suppose Clark Kent and Superman are the same man. Then if Clark Kent has dark hair and works at the *Daily Planet*, so does Superman, since there is only one man for those facts to be about. This principle is called **Leibniz's law**, after Gottfried Leibniz, and it says that if A is identical with B, then whatever is true of A is true of B.

The law gives us a test for telling two things apart: find something that is true of one and not of the other. If one house has a red door and the house across the road has none, they cannot be the same house. It runs from identity to shared properties, and it does **not** claim that two things with the same properties must be identical.

René Descartes held that the mind and the body are different kinds of thing, and one way of reading his reasoning starts from doubt. In the First and Second Meditations he finds that he can doubt that his body exists, since he might be dreaming it or deceived about it by a [[sceptical hypothesis|A scenario in which everything would seem as it does and your beliefs be systematically wrong. Met in 'Dreams, demons and closure'.]], but that he cannot doubt that he himself exists, because doubting is a kind of *thinking* and there must be someone doing it. Add Leibniz's law and the conclusion seems to follow: if he were identical with his body, whatever was true of his body would be true of him, and he could not doubt the one while being certain of the other.

**Substance dualism** is the view that there are two kinds of substance, mind, whose nature is to think, and matter, whose nature is to take up space. A substance, in the old sense of the word, is a thing that exists in its own right and not merely as a feature of something else.

steps.headline: Does the doubt argument survive the Lois case?

workedSteps.text: The Lois argument has true premises in the story and a false conclusion, so it is invalid, even though it looks just like an application of [[Leibniz's law|If A is identical with B, whatever is true of A is true of B. Met in 'Mind and body'.]].
It fails because “believed by Lois to fly” is not a property of the man himself. It describes Lois's state of mind, and her state of mind can differ between the two names for him.
Now compare Descartes's property of “being doubted by me”. Ask yourself what the Lois case suggests about it.

The doubt argument therefore stands or falls on whether being doubted is a feature of the body itself or only of how I think about it. The French theologian Antoine Arnauld raised a similar objection to Descartes in the Objections published with the Meditations.

lead.text: A body is **extended**, which means that it takes up space, with a length, a breadth and a depth, while a mind on his view is not extended at all. Yet a thought can lead to an action, since deciding to raise your arm is followed by your arm rising, and so the mind *seems* to act on the body.

In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote to Descartes pressing exactly this point. She asked how the soul, being only a thinking and unextended thing, could determine the movements of the body, given that all movement we know of involves one thing pushing another by contact. Descartes replied that the union of mind and body is something we know through ordinary life more than through reasoning, and Elisabeth was not satisfied. The difficulty is now called the **interaction problem**.

Elisabeth's challenge can be set out as an argument in three premises: if the mind moves the body, it touches the body; if the mind touches the body, it is extended; and the mind is not extended. The conclusion is that the mind does not move the body. The reasoning chains the first two premises into “if the mind moves the body, it is extended” and then denies the second half, which is the form you met in the last lessons.

That means the argument is valid, and **a dualist cannot answer by pointing to a flaw in its logic**. There are three ways to reply, each of which gives up a premise: deny that moving something requires touching it, deny that touching requires extension, or accept that the mind has some kind of extension after all. Each costs the dualist something, and the first two ask us to believe in causes that *do not work by contact*.

lead.text: **Physicalism** is the view that everything there is, minds included, is physical. A modern argument for it starts from the thought that every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause, so that a movement of your arm is already fully caused by events in your nerves and muscles. If some mental events cause physical events as well, and the physical events are not caused twice over, then those mental events *must* themselves be physical.

In the 1950s U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart proposed the **identity theory**: each type of mental state, such as being in pain, simply is a type of brain state, in the way that lightning is an electrical discharge. **Property dualism** takes a middle path. It agrees that there is only one kind of substance, the physical, but holds that mental properties, such as how pain feels, are not physical properties.

afterFigure.text: The physicalist escapes the interaction problem by denying that the mind is a separate thing to be moved, though at the price of having to say what becomes of how experiences feel.

blocks.text: Are you the same thing as your body? In one sense the answer is plainly yes, since you have hands and a heart and you are the one who is hungry. In another it is less clear, because the thoughts you are having now do not seem to be located anywhere in your body the way your hands are. René Descartes thought the difference was real, that a mind is one kind of thing and a body another.

If he is right, a second problem appears at once, because a mind with no size, shape or position still has to move the arm that reaches for a cup, and it is far from clear how something unextended could push anything.

recap.keyIdea: Descartes's doubt argument depends on a debatable use of Leibniz's law, and the interaction problem shows how costly substance dualism is, which is why physicalist alternatives are attractive.

blocks.text: Descartes argued that because he could doubt his body but not his own existence, the two are not identical, and from this he derived **substance dualism**. The argument uses Leibniz's law, and the Superman case shows why it is shaky, since a property such as being doubted by me may describe my attitude and not the thing.

Princess Elisabeth's *interaction problem* asks how an unextended mind could move an extended body, and the argument she gave is valid. Physicalists avoid the problem by identifying the mind with the brain, while property dualists keep one substance but hold that mental properties are not physical.

lessons.title: Function and the Chinese Room

lead.text: Take the question about the two adders seriously. A gear-driven adding machine and a pocket calculator have nothing in common in how they are built, and yet both are adding, because adding is something that is *done*, and anything that reliably turns 3 and 4 into 7 is doing it. A good many ordinary kinds work like this. A mousetrap is anything that catches mice, whether it is made of wood and a spring or of plastic and a lever, and a clock is anything that keeps time. Kinds of this sort are defined by their job, or **function**, and not by their material.

This matters in the philosophy of mind, because the view you met last lesson ties each kind of mental state to a kind of brain state. If mental kinds are defined by their jobs instead, the match could be much looser: a creature with no neurons might still have a state that does the job that pain does in us.

Take a drinks machine of the kind Ned Block used when he introduced this idea to philosophers, which sells a can for 20p and accepts 10p and 20p coins. It is always in one of two states, nothing owed (S0) or 10p credited (S1), and the table says what it does for each state and each coin. In S0 a 10p moves it to S1 with no output, and a 20p gives a can and leaves it in S0. In S1 a 10p completes the price and gives a can, and a 20p gives a can and 10p change. A list that gives, for every state and every input, the next state and the output is called a **machine table**.

S1 is not a part of the machine, and it is not a coin in a tray. It is *whatever condition* the machine is in such that a further 10p brings out a can. A **functional state** is a state defined in this way, by its place in the table: by what it does with each input and by which state it leads to.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the same table realised twice, once in gears and levers and once in silicon chips. The two machines differ in every physical detail, yet whenever 10p has been credited each is in the same functional state, because that is all the table asks.

steps.headline: Running the table on three coins

The second coin is also a 10p, but this time the machine is in S1, and a can comes out. Ask yourself why the same coin has done something different.
That can leaves the machine back in S0, and the 20p arrives there. In S0 a 20p buys a can at once and leaves the machine in S0.
Two cans have come out. The first two coins were identical, so the difference between a coin that waits and a coin that buys comes entirely from the state the machine was in.

lead.text: **Functionalism** is the view that a mental state is defined by its causal role: by what typically causes it, how it interacts with other mental states, and what behaviour it produces. Pain, on this view, is whatever state is caused by bodily damage, leads to distress and a wish for it to stop, and produces wincing and avoidance.

That is why functionalism is awkward for the [[identity theory|The view that each type of mental state is a type of brain state. Met in 'Mind and body'.]]. Hilary Putnam argued in the 1960s that if pain were identical with one kind of brain state, then a creature with a different brain, such as an octopus, could not feel pain, which seems *wrong*. It seems more likely that **multiple realisability** holds: one mental kind can be realised in many different physical systems, in the way that the drinks machine's table can be realised in gears, in neurons or in silicon.

afterFigure.text: If a state is defined by its role, and silicon can play the role, then silicon can be in that state, and so it is natural to ask whether a computer running the right program could really think.

lead.text: In 1980, in a paper called “Minds, Brains, and Programs”, John Searle described the best-known objection to the idea that a computer could think. Imagine a man who understands no Chinese, shut in a room with a very large rulebook, written in English, and trays of Chinese characters. Slips of Chinese writing are passed in, and he finds their shapes in the rulebook, which tells him which characters to pass back out. The rulebook is so good that the replies are indistinguishable from those of a native speaker. To the people outside, the room understands Chinese. To the man inside, the characters are just *meaningless* squiggles.

The rulebook is a machine table: given the state of the conversation and the symbol that comes in, it says which symbols to send out. Searle's target was **strong AI**, the claim that an appropriately programmed computer literally understands. The man runs the program and understands nothing, so Searle concluded that running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding. He put the reason as a contrast between syntax and semantics: a program deals in the shapes of symbols, while understanding requires what they mean.

The commonest reply says that Searle is looking in the wrong place. It may be true that the man understands no Chinese, the objection goes, but he is only one part of a system that also includes the rulebook, the trays and the papers, and it is the whole system that understands, in the way that no single neuron in your head understands English although you do. This is the **systems reply**.

Searle answered that the man could memorise the whole rulebook and do *all* the work in his head, so that the system would be nothing but the man, and he would still understand no Chinese. Defenders of the systems reply doubt that this settles it, since a person who has internalised such a rulebook might be running a second mind that the first one knows nothing about.

If minds turn out to resemble adders, a startling possibility opens up, which is that something made of silicon might think. John Searle argued in 1980 that it could not, and the argument it started has not been settled.

blocks.text: A **machine table** gives, for each state and input, the next state and the output, and a *functional state* is defined by its place in the table and not by what the machine is made of. **Functionalism** applies this to the mind, and so a mental state can be *multiply realised* in neurons, gears or silicon.

Searle's Chinese Room grants that a program could produce fluent replies and argues that the man running it still understands nothing, so that running a program is not sufficient for understanding. The systems reply answers that understanding belongs to the whole room, and the dispute has not been settled.

lessons.title: What makes you you

lead.text: The question of **personal identity** asks what makes a person at one time the same person as someone at another time. An answer takes the form of a **criterion of identity**: a condition which, when it holds between the child and you, makes them one and the same.

The most natural first answer is the **bodily criterion**, according to which a person at a later time is the same person as one at an earlier time just when they have the same living body. It handles the photograph well, since a body can stay the same through gradual change in the way a river does, and nobody doubts that your body is continuous with the child's. Its difficulty is that it seems to give the *wrong* verdict in cases where what matters to us is not the body.

John Locke thought the body was the wrong place to look. In the second edition of his *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1694) he added a chapter on identity, in which a person is a thinking, intelligent being that can consider itself as the same thing at different times and places, and what makes it the same, he argued, is consciousness. His example was a prince whose soul, with all of the prince's memories, enters the body of a cobbler. Everyone, Locke thought, would say that the person in the cobbler's body is the prince, even though the body is the cobbler's.

This gives the **memory criterion**: a person at one time is the same person as one at an earlier time just when they can remember that earlier person's experiences from the inside. It helps to speak of **stages**, a person as they are at one particular time, so that the criterion becomes a rule about which stages belong together.

Thomas Reid, in his *Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man* (1785), objected to Locke with a story. A boy is flogged for robbing an orchard. Later, as a young officer, he takes a standard, the enemy's flag, in his first campaign, and later still he becomes a general. Suppose that the officer remembers being flogged as a boy, and that the general remembers taking the standard but **has forgotten the flogging**.

afterFigure.text: In the first view each neighbouring pair is joined by memory, and in the second the same three stages are joined only by the body they share. The memory criterion looks at the first kind of link, and the story is built to find out what it says when the links do not reach all the way along.

cases.label: The same three stages, by body

workedSteps.text: Take the criterion one pair at a time. The officer remembers the boy's flogging from the inside, so the officer is the boy.
The general remembers the officer's deed from the inside, so the general is the officer.
The general has forgotten the flogging, so the criterion also says that the general is not the boy. Ask yourself why that is a problem.
Reid took this to show that the criterion cannot be what identity consists in, since it says that the general is the officer, that the officer is the boy, and that the general is not the boy.

lead.text: Identity has a property that the memory criterion lacks. It is **transitive**: if A is the same as B and B is the same as C, then A is the same as C. The criterion fails this test because it demands that the later stage remember the earlier one directly, and memory *runs out* well before a long life does, so that the old general cannot reach the boy although each is linked to the officer.

The repair keeps Locke's idea and counts chains. The **continuity view** says that a later stage is the same person as an earlier one when the two are joined by an overlapping chain of memory, so that the general reaches the boy through the officer. Views of this kind, which follow memory and later also character and intentions, are called **psychological criteria**.

afterFigure.text: The second view in the figure shows a longer life, with four stages in a row, each remembering only the one before. No direct link reaches from the last to the first, but the chain of overlapping links does, and the continuity view counts all four stages as one person.

reveal.text: B is linked to A directly and C is linked to A through B, but no memory joins D to C, so the chain stops at C and D is left out. Two of the three stages count.

workedSteps.text: Take a child A of 10, and then B, C and D at 30, 50 and 80. B remembers A's experiences and C remembers B's but not A's, while D, after an illness, remembers nothing of A's, B's or C's experiences.
On the direct memory criterion only B would count, since only B remembers A's experiences itself. On the continuity view we follow the chain instead.
Link by link, count how many of B, C and D are the same person as A.

lead.text: Derek Parfit, in *Reasons and Persons* (1984), pressed a harder case against the continuity view. Suppose that your brain is divided and each half is transplanted into a new body, so that the two survivors, Lefty and Righty, both remember your life and have your character. This is a case of **fission**, where one person divides into two. Both survivors are psychologically continuous with you, so on the continuity view each of them is you.

That cannot be right, because identity is one-one. If Lefty is you and Righty is you, then Lefty is Righty, and yet they are two people with two bodies who will go their separate ways. The continuity view can avoid the contradiction only by adding a clause such as “provided that nobody else is also continuous with you”, which makes whether you survive depend on a fact about a stranger.

afterFigure.text: He argued that identity is not what matters in survival: what matters is psychological continuity itself, which can hold to a degree and can branch, and in the fission case each survivor has everything we care about in our own future.

lead.text: Parfit built a case in which the criteria come apart. In his teletransporter, you step into a scanner on Earth, which records the state of every cell in your body and destroys it, and the information is used to build an exact **replica** on Mars. On a psychological criterion the replica is continuous with you, and so the machine is simply a way of travelling. The bodily criterion asks a different question, which is whether the body that stepped into the scanner on Earth is the body that walks out on Mars.
In the branch-line version the scanner copies you but fails to destroy your body, so that you are still on Earth when the replica wakes on Mars.

afterFigure.text: The bodily criterion says the person on Earth is you, and the replica is someone else. The psychological criterion gives both of you a claim, which is the fission problem over again.

blocks.text: Look at a photograph of yourself at six, and say whether the child in it is you. You will say yes without hesitation, and yet the child had different beliefs and different tastes, and a body made largely of cells that are no longer there. What exactly are you saying when you say that the child is you, and what would have to happen to make you wrong?

The question stops being academic once we imagine cases that pull the usual answers apart: a memory that fades, a brain that splits in two, a machine that copies you and destroys the original. Philosophers use such cases to ask what, if anything, makes a person the same person from one day to the next.

intro.whyItMatters: What we think survival requires decides what we fear, promise and take responsibility for.

recap.keyIdea: The bodily and memory criteria give rival answers about who is the same person, Reid's case shows that direct memory fails transitivity, and Parfit's cases suggest that continuity is what matters.

blocks.text: The **bodily criterion** follows the living body, while Locke's **memory criterion** follows what a later stage remembers of an earlier one. Reid's brave officer shows that direct memory fails *transitivity*, and the continuity view repairs it by counting overlapping chains of memory.

Parfit's fission case shows that continuity can branch, which identity cannot, and the teleporter shows how far the two criteria can disagree. He concluded that what matters in survival is continuity and not identity.

lessons.title: Counting consequences

lead.text: **Consequentialism** says that the rightness of an act depends only on how good its consequences are, so that the right act is the one with the best results. To compare results we need a measure of how good they are, and consequentialists usually take it to be **welfare**, how well people's lives go: their happiness, their health, the absence of pain.

The theory has to rank acts under uncertainty. The standard way is to weight each possible outcome by its probability and add the results, and the total is the act's **expected utility**. Suppose a game pays 12 points if you roll a six and nothing otherwise. A six comes up one time in six, so over many rolls you win on average 1/6 × 12 = 2 points per roll, even though no single roll *ever* pays exactly 2. That average is the game's expected utility, and a consequentialist ranks acts by it.

In the figure, option A is a modest gamble, with a 90% chance of 60 units and a 10% chance of 20, so its expected utility is 0.9 × 60 + 0.1 × 20 = 54 + 2 = 56. Option B is bold, with a 50% chance of 120 units and a 50% chance of nothing, so its expected utility is 0.5 × 120 = 60. B has the higher total, and a consequentialist who ranks acts by expected utility chooses it, even though it is the one *more likely* to leave us with nothing.

afterFigure.text: Switch to the second view, where B succeeds only 40% of the time. Its expected utility falls to 0.4 × 120 = 48, which is below 56, and A is now the better choice. The rule is always the same: **compute the weighted total for each option and take the largest**.

cases.label: Modest gamble against a bold one
The bold gamble succeeds less often
Modest gamble against a bold one

lead.text: Most acts risk harm as well as promising benefit, and the theory handles harm in the simplest possible way, by **giving it a negative value**. A harm of 30 units with a probability of 0.1 contributes 0.1 × (−30) = −3.

This means that a likely small benefit can be outweighed by an unlikely large harm. An act that gives 10 units with probability 0.9 and costs 100 units with probability 0.1 has an expected utility of 9 − 10 = −1, and the consequentialist should decline it although it will *usually* turn out well.

steps.headline: A treatment with a benefit and a harm

workedSteps.text: A treatment gives a benefit of 10 units with probability 0.7, and causes a harm of 20 units with probability 0.3. The benefit's weighted value is 0.7 × 10 = 7.
The harm is written as −20, because it subtracts from the total. Ask yourself why it takes a minus sign.
Its weighted value is 0.3 × (−20) = −6.
The expected utility is 7 + (−6) = 1, so the treatment is only just worth giving. Doing nothing has an expected utility of 0, and 1 is higher.

reveal.text: Doing nothing has an expected utility of 0, so running the programme is better. In the riskier version, which works only 60% of the time, the weighted values are 12 and −12, and the programme is no better than doing nothing.

workedSteps.text: A vaccination programme works with probability 0.9, giving a benefit of 20 units, and causes side effects with probability 0.1, giving a harm of 30 units. The weighted benefit is 0.9 × 20 = 18.
The side effects count as −30, so their weighted value is 0.1 × (−30) = −3.
Add the two weighted values to find the programme's expected utility.

lead.text: The classical answer is **utilitarianism**, the consequentialist view that the good is happiness and that everyone's happiness counts equally. John Stuart Mill, whose *Utilitarianism* appeared in 1861, called the standard the **greatest happiness principle**: actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness.

Mill held that pleasures differ in quality as well as in amount. “It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied,” he wrote, “better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.”

In 1967 Philippa Foot raised a case that has since become known as the trolley problem: a runaway tram will kill five people unless the driver steers it onto a side track, where it will kill one. For a utilitarian the question is answered by counting. If we measure welfare in lives only, one act leaves five dead, the other leaves one dead, and **the act with the smaller loss is the right one**.

afterFigure.text: Changing the numbers changes the margin by which one option beats the other, though not which way it goes, as long as the main track holds more people.

cases.label: Five ahead, one on the side
Three ahead, one on the side

lead.text: T. M. Scanlon, in *What We Owe to Each Other* (1998), described a case of this kind. Jones has had an accident in the transmitter room of a television station, and he can be freed only by interrupting the broadcast, for fifteen minutes, while a match that millions are watching has an hour left to run. Waiting means an hour of terrible pain for Jones.

A utilitarian adds up welfare across people. Each viewer loses only a little, but there are millions of them, and with the numbers in the figure the sum of their losses (−60 thousand units) exceeds Jones's (−40 thousand), so the sum says to let Jones suffer. Summing welfare across people in this way is called **aggregation**.

afterFigure.text: The second view reduces the audience to thousands, and the total falls to −6 thousand units, so the sum now says to rescue Jones. Nothing in the theory marks a point at which Jones's claim cannot be outweighed, and Scanlon's complaint is that it should be: however many small losses we add up, none of the viewers has a claim as strong as his.

lessons.orientation: Rank acts by their expected outcomes, and see where summing welfare across people gives troubling verdicts.
