blocks.text: Should a health service run a vaccination programme that will very probably protect many people but might harm a few? Most of us would want to know two things before answering: how good and how bad the possible outcomes are, and how likely each of them is. One tradition in ethics says that those two things settle the matter, that the right act is simply the one that turns out best overall, and it offers a way of comparing acts by arithmetic.

The same arithmetic also produces verdicts that many people find hard to accept, such as letting one person suffer badly when enough others each gain a little, and you can only judge those verdicts once you can see exactly what the theory is counting.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out an act's expected utility, with harms counted as negatives, and explain where aggregation gives troubling verdicts.
intro.whyItMatters: The arithmetic of outcomes is the clearest way to see what consequentialism commits you to.

recap.keyIdea: Consequentialism ranks acts by the expected value of their outcomes, and utilitarian aggregation can let many small gains outweigh one great harm.

blocks.text: A **consequentialist** ranks acts by their *expected utility*: each outcome's welfare, weighted by its probability and added up, with harms counted as negative numbers. The classical form is utilitarianism, with Bentham counting pleasure and pain and Mill's greatest happiness principle adding a difference in the quality of pleasures.

The same arithmetic **aggregates** welfare across people, so that in Scanlon's transmitter room many small losses can outweigh one man's great one. Whether that verdict is a discovery or a reductio, a sign that something in the theory has gone wrong, is the question the next lesson takes up.

lessons.title: Duty, persons and the footbridge

lead.text: If we count lives, the two cases are identical: five die if you do nothing and one dies if you act, so a strict utilitarian has to treat them alike. Most people do not, and the puzzle is to say what the difference could be.

One candidate is the part that the one person's death plays in your plan. In the lever case the man on the side track is simply unlucky, since if he were absent pulling the lever would still save the five, and so his death is a foreseen **side effect**: something you expect but do not need. In the footbridge case the plan works only because of the stranger's body, which is what stops the trolley. When a person's fate is what your plan uses to succeed, he is a **means**.

afterFigure.text: The count does not change between the views, and what changes is the *place* of that one person in the plan.

lead.text: In the *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785) he argued that a person has a worth that is not a price. Things with a price can be exchanged for something of equal value, whereas a person has dignity and cannot be traded for any amount of anything else. This gives one of his statements of the moral law: act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always at the same time as an end, and never merely as a means. A person is an **end in itself**, someone whose own reason and aims you must respect, and this statement is called the **formula of humanity**.

The word “merely” matters, because we use one another as means all the time, as when we buy a ticket from a clerk, and Kant has no objection to that. His complaint is about using someone *only* as a tool, in a way they could not agree to.

afterFigure.text: Kant never considered trolleys, so applying the formula to them is an extension of his principle and not a verdict of his own. It is a natural extension all the same, because it explains why the footbridge feels different from the lever.

workedSteps.text: Take the footbridge plan: stop the trolley by pushing the stranger in front of it. To see whether he is a means, remove him from the picture and ask what happens to the plan.

Without him nothing stops the trolley and the five die, so the plan needs his body, and he is used as a means. In the lever case, by contrast, the plan works whether or not anyone stands on the side track.
Both plans have the same count of lives. Ask yourself why it should matter morally that one of them needs the person's body.
On Kant's principle, a plan that needs someone's body, without his agreement, treats him merely as a tool. In the lever case the one person is harmed, but the plan does not use him.
The footbridge plan needs the stranger's body, so it uses him as a means, and he has not agreed to be used.
Kant's principle says that a person must always be treated as an end in itself and never merely as a means.
Name the formula of Kant's moral law that this principle gives.

lead.text: Anything you do rests on a **maxim**, the rule you are acting on: for example, “when I need money, I will promise to repay it, knowing that I cannot.” The **formula of universal law** says to act only on a maxim that you could at the same time will to become a universal law. If everyone made promises they knew they could not keep, no one would believe a promise to repay, and then the maxim could not even be acted on, since there would be nobody left to deceive. A maxim that *undermines itself* when everyone adopts it is forbidden.

afterFigure.text: If everyone repays, promises stay credible, and you can will it as a universal law.

premises.text: My maxim: when I need money, I will promise to repay it, knowing I cannot.
If everyone acted on this maxim, no one would believe a promise to repay.
If no one believed such promises, the maxim could not be acted on.

conclusion.text: I cannot will the maxim as a universal law, so the false promise is forbidden.

premises.text: My maxim: when I borrow money, I will repay it as promised.
If everyone acted on this maxim, promises to repay would remain credible.

conclusion.text: I can will this maxim as a universal law.

lead.text: “If you want to be trusted, keep your promises” is a command, but a conditional one: it applies *only* to someone who wants to be trusted, and a person who does not care about trust is free to ignore it. Kant calls commands of this kind **hypothetical imperatives**, because they say what to do given a goal. A **categorical imperative** binds you whatever you want, and its force does not depend on any goal you happen to have.

The formula of universal law and the formula of humanity are both categorical, and if either is right, then neither “but I don't care about that” nor “but it would produce better results” is an answer to it.

The **doctrine of double effect**, traced to Thomas Aquinas's discussion of self-defence in the *Summa Theologiae*, holds that it can be permissible to bring about a harm as a foreseen side effect of a good act, though not to intend harm as a means to a good end. Applied to the trolley, it permits the lever, where the death is a side effect, and forbids the push, where the death is the means.

Judith Jarvis Thomson, who gave the trolley problem its name and added the footbridge, also devised a case to test the doctrine. In her loop case the side track rejoins the main line, so the trolley, once diverted, would come round and kill the five unless the one person on the loop stops it. His body is now needed, which makes his death a means.

afterFigure.text: The doctrine says that diverting the trolley is forbidden here, as in the footbridge, but many people still find it permissible, which some philosophers take to count against the doctrine, and others take to show that the distinction needs refining.

blocks.text: A runaway trolley will kill five people unless you divert it, and diverting it kills one. Most people say that pulling the lever is permissible. Now suppose the only way to stop the trolley is to push a heavy stranger off a footbridge so that his body blocks it. The count is the same, five lives against one, and yet most people say that pushing him is wrong.

If the arithmetic is identical, what could the difference be? Last lesson's theory has no answer, since it looks only at totals, and so philosophers have looked for one in what the act does to the person, and in the kind of rule that the act follows.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say why the lever and the footbridge differ, apply Kant's universal-law and humanity formulas, and explain the doctrine of double effect.
intro.whyItMatters: These principles explain why some acts seem forbidden whatever the totals say.

recap.keyIdea: Kantian ethics and the doctrine of double effect both treat using a person as a means differently from causing harm as a side effect, which explains why the footbridge and the lever feel different.

blocks.text: The lever and the footbridge have the same count of lives, but in one case the death of the one is a **side effect** and in the other it is a **means**. Kant's *formula of humanity* forbids treating a person merely as a means, and his *formula of universal law* asks whether everyone could act on your maxim.

The doctrine of double effect draws the same line from a different tradition, and Thomson's loop case shows that the line is contested. A categorical imperative binds whatever you want, and that is why these principles can forbid an act whose totals look best.

lessons.title: Character and the mean

lead.text: Suppose ten minae of food (a mina was a Greek unit of weight) is too much for a person, and two is too little. The figure halfway between is the **arithmetic mean** of the two amounts, found by adding them and halving the total, so that the arithmetic mean of 4 and 10 is (4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 7.
It takes no notice of who is eating, and so it is the same for everyone. For Aristotle's own numbers, ten minae and two, it is six.

Aristotle's answer is that the trainer will not necessarily prescribe six, because six may be too much for the person who is to eat it or too little. It would be too little for Milo of Croton, the celebrated wrestler, and too much for a beginner in athletic training. What counts as the right amount is therefore not a fixed point between the extremes: it depends on *who* is eating, and Aristotle called it the **mean relative to us**, as against the arithmetic mean, which is the same for everyone.

afterFigure.text: Milo's right amount is the band from 7 to 9, and the beginner's is the band from 3 to 5. Six lies below Milo's band and above the beginner's, so it is the wrong amount for each of them, and for opposite reasons.

lead.text: A **virtue** is a settled state of character that disposes us to feel and act as we should. Take courage, which concerns fear and confidence. Someone with too little confidence, who flees from every danger, is a coward, and someone with too much, who rushes into danger without thought, is rash. Each fault is a **vice**: the one that falls short of the right amount is a **deficiency**, and the one that goes beyond it is an **excess**.

Being a mean does not make a virtue mediocre. Aristotle says that in respect of what is best and right a virtue is an *extreme*, and it is a mean only in the sense that it lies between two ways of going wrong.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows that the band for courage is different for a trained firefighter and for an untrained passer-by, which is the mean relative to us at work in a virtue.

steps.headline: The same virtue in two people

workedSteps.text: Both a trained firefighter and an untrained passer-by face a fire. On the scale of confidence from 0 to 10, the right amount for the firefighter is the band from 6 to 8, and for the passer-by the band from 3 to 5.
Take a confidence of 7. For the firefighter it is within the band, so it is courage, while for the passer-by it is above the band, so it is rashness.
The same level of confidence is virtuous in one person and a vice in the other. Ask yourself why the two bands differ.
The scale and the virtue are the same for both, and the people are different, with different training and different things they can rightly do.

lead.text: Truthfulness about yourself lies between boastfulness, which claims more than you have, and mock modesty, which claims less. Good temper lies between irascibility, anger that is too easily roused, and lack of spirit, a failure to be angry when anger is called for. Each virtue concerns some feeling or action that can come in *degrees*, and has **a vice on either side of it**.

afterFigure.text: Someone jostled in a queue should feel only a little, and the right band is low, while a parent whose child is being harmed should feel a great deal more. Aristotle thought that some things have no mean at all, such as spite, and murder or theft as actions, because they are wrong however they are done, and so his view is about the virtues that concern feelings and actions of degree.

workedSteps.text: Generosity concerns giving money. A person who gives too much, wasting what they have, shows prodigality, which is the vice of excess.
The virtue lies between this fault and a second one, as courage lies between rashness and cowardice.
Name the second fault, the vice of deficiency, which gives too little.

lead.text: Aristotle distinguishes the virtues of thought, which we acquire by teaching, from the virtues of character, which come from **habituation**. We become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, and brave by doing brave acts, in the way that people become builders by building and lyre players by playing.

This means that being told what courage is will not make anyone courageous. It also means that the right kind of practice matters: facing danger in doses that we can manage and in the right spirit shifts a person's band towards courage, while repeated flight builds cowardice and repeated recklessness builds rashness.

Aristotle's answer is **practical wisdom**, in Greek *phronesis*: the ability, built up by experience, to see in a particular case what the right amount is. He defines a virtue as a state lying in the mean, as determined by the reasoning of the practically wise person.

Aristotle held that the highest human good is **eudaimonia**, usually translated as happiness or flourishing, which he described as an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. A virtue is not a tool for getting something else, such as pleasure, but is part of what living well consists in.

blocks.text: We praise courage, generosity and a good temper, so is it possible to have too much of them? We have words for people who go too far: reckless, wasteful, hot-headed. It seems that a quality can be good in the right amount and bad beyond it, which raises the question of what the right amount is and who decides.

Aristotle took the question seriously, and he tried it first on a very ordinary case, how much an athlete in training should eat, where there is plainly an amount that is too much and an amount that is too little. The way he settled that case became the model for his whole account of character, which tells you how to find the right amount of a quality in a situation that no rule foresaw.

intro.whyItMatters: Virtue ethics asks what kind of person to be, and that depends on the situation as well as on a rule.

recap.keyIdea: A virtue lies in a mean between a deficiency and an excess, the mean is relative to the person and the situation, and character is acquired by habit.

blocks.text: A **virtue** lies between two vices, one of deficiency and one of excess, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness. The mean is *relative to us*, not the arithmetic midpoint: six minae is too little for Milo and too much for a beginner.

Character comes from **habituation**, from doing the right kind of act again and again, and *practical wisdom* is the skill of seeing the mean in each case. All of this serves eudaimonia, a life of activity in accordance with virtue.

lessons.title: The social contract

lead.text: Philosophers call the condition of people with no government a **state of nature**, and the first great answer to what it would be like comes from Thomas Hobbes, in *Leviathan* (1651). He also thought that competition for scarce goods, fear of one another and the desire for reputation would set them against one another, and that where nothing keeps them all in awe, the result is a war of every man against every man. In such a condition, he thought, there would be no farming, no trade, no arts and no society, and worst of all a continual fear of violent death.

His remedy is for people to make an agreement with one another, each giving up the freedom to do whatever they think necessary to survive, in return for safety. They agree to obey a **sovereign**, a common power with the authority to enforce the peace, and the agreement is a **social contract**.

premises.text: Without a common power, each person may do whatever preserves himself.
Even the weakest can kill the strongest, by plot or alliance.
Competition, fear and pride make conflict likely.

conclusion.text: Without a sovereign, life is a war of all against all.

premises.text: In the state of nature a law of nature already forbids harming others.
People leave it only to secure their lives, liberties and property.

conclusion.text: Government is legitimate only by consent, and only within those limits.

lead.text: John Locke, in the *Second Treatise of Government* (published in 1689), imagined the state of nature very differently. It is not lawless, he said: a **law of nature**, which reason can discover, already tells everyone that no one ought to harm another in life, health, liberty or possessions. The trouble is that each person is the judge in their own case, which makes disputes hard to settle fairly. People therefore agree to form a government, to protect their lives, liberties and property, and its authority rests on their **consent**.

A government's power reaches only as far as the purpose for which people agreed to it, and if it turns against the lives, liberties and property that it was set up to protect, Locke argued, the people may replace it.

premises.text: Without a common power, each person may do whatever preserves himself.
Even the weakest can kill the strongest, by plot or alliance.
Competition, fear and pride make conflict likely.

conclusion.text: Without a sovereign, life is a war of all against all.

premises.text: In the state of nature a law of nature already forbids harming others.
People leave it only to secure their lives, liberties and property.

conclusion.text: Government is legitimate only by consent, and only within those limits.

lead.text: In *A Theory of Justice* (1971) John Rawls used the idea differently, as a test of fairness. Imagine that you are choosing the basic rules of a society, but that you do not know what your place in it will be: whether you will be rich or poor, strong or weak, talented or not. Rawls calls this ignorance the **veil of ignorance**, and the imagined situation of choice behind it the original position.
The idea is that rules chosen behind the veil cannot be tailored to the advantage of the person choosing, since the chooser does not know who that will be.
A small case shows how choosing without knowing your share changes what you want.

Suppose that behind the veil you are comparing two societies, and all you know about each is the income of each of three equal groups, from the lowest third to the top third, and that you are equally likely to land in any of them. One reasonable rule is to prefer the society with the higher **expected income**, which with equal chances of each group is simply the average of the three incomes. Another is the **maximin** rule, which looks at the worst position in each society and chooses the society whose worst position is best. The name is short for maximising the minimum.

In the figure, society P pays its groups 20, 30 and 40, and society Q pays 12, 30 and 48. Both averages are 30, so the average cannot choose between them, but maximin does, since P's worst-off group gets 20 and Q's gets 12.

afterFigure.text: The second view compares P with R, which pays 25, 30 and 35. The averages are again equal at 30, and maximin chooses R. A rule that looks only at the average is *blind* to the spread, and maximin is a rule that cares about it.

workedSteps.text: Compare society A, which pays its three equal groups 10, 40 and 70, with society C, which pays 20, 45 and 95. First the averages: A gives (10 + 40 + 70) ÷ 3 = 40, and C gives (20 + 45 + 95) ÷ 3 = 160 ÷ 3, which is about 53.
Now the worst positions: A's lowest group gets 10 and C's gets 20. Maximin therefore chooses C, and so does the average.
Both rules choose the same society, so there is no tension between them here. Ask yourself why.
A dilemma arises only when one society has the higher average and the other has the higher worst position, which is what happens when A is compared with a flatter society.

lead.text: With groups of unequal size the expected income has to **weight** each income by the share of people who receive it. This gives a **weighted average**. In the figure, a quarter of the people receive 20 units in society X and three quarters receive 60, so the expected income is 0.25 × 20 + 0.75 × 60 = 5 + 45 = 50. Maximin takes no notice of the shares: it still looks only at the lowest income, 20 in X against 28 in Y.

Rawls argued that parties behind the veil would choose maximin, and his rule for society is the **difference principle**: social and economic inequalities are permitted only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. It does not demand equal incomes, but it allows an inequality *only when* the worst-off gain from it.

afterFigure.text: John Harsanyi argued the opposite, that parties behind the veil would maximise the average, which brings us back to the consequentialist's totals.

lessons.orientation: Compare Hobbes's and Locke's social contracts, then choose principles behind Rawls's veil of ignorance with maximin and averages.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Every government claims the right to make rules for you and to punish you for breaking them, though you never signed anything agreeing to that. What could give it the right? One way in is to ask what life would be like with no government at all, and which picture you find more believable, people carrying on much as before or people falling upon one another, says a good deal about what you think people are like.

Philosophers have given both answers, and each carries a different view of what a government is for and of when you could rightly stop obeying it. A modern version of the question asks which rules you would choose for a society if you did not know which person in it you would be, and that question can be answered with some surprisingly simple arithmetic.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compare Hobbes's and Locke's social contracts, and choose between two societies behind Rawls's veil of ignorance by the average and by maximin.
intro.whyItMatters: How you answer decides what a government is for and when it can lose your obedience.

recap.keyIdea: Hobbes grounds a strong sovereign in fear, Locke grounds a limited government in consent, and Rawls asks what principles you would choose without knowing your place, where maximin and the average can disagree.

blocks.text: For Hobbes the **state of nature** is a war of all against all, and the **social contract** creates a sovereign to end it, while for Locke a *law of nature* already binds people and government rests on **consent** within limits. Rawls turns the contract into a test of fairness: choose the rules behind the **veil of ignorance**.

There you can compare societies by *expected income* or by **maximin**, which looks at the worst position, and the two rules sometimes choose differently. Rawls's difference principle is the maximin idea applied to a society, and Harsanyi's reply is that the average should decide.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. You have read arguments, tested them, and met the main questions of knowledge, mind and ethics that they are used to answer.

questions.prompt: Read this passage: “Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.” How many premises does it state?
hints: Find the claim the passage wants you to accept; that is the conclusion.
“Since” introduces the reasons. List each separate claim it introduces.
Count the claims offered as reasons, leaving out the conclusion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the bridge's date of construction, and the rule that bridges of that age must be inspected this year. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: The bridge's age and the inspection rule are the two reasons, and the last clause, that the bridge must be inspected this year, is what they support.

misconceptions.feedback: That count includes the conclusion. Count only the claims offered as reasons for it.
Look at the “and” inside the “since” clause. It joins two separate claims, and each is offered as a reason.

questions.prompt: In the passage “The council should not sell the playing field. After all, it is the only open space in the ward, and selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's own planning policy.”, which statement is the conclusion?
hints: Ask which statement the speaker wants you to accept.
“After all” introduces reasons. What are they reasons for?

acceptedIdeas: The council should not sell the playing field.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The council should not sell the playing field.

choices.label: Selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's own planning policy.
It is the only open space in the ward.
The council should not sell the playing field.

questions.onCorrect: “After all” marks what follows it as reasons, so the statement they are offered for is the conclusion, even though it comes first.

misconceptions.feedback: “After all” introduces that statement as a reason, so it is offered in support of something else, namely that the council should not sell the field.
That statement is joined to the reason before it by “and”, so it is a second reason, and both are offered for the claim that the council should not sell the field.

questions.prompt: What is the traditional name for an argument that leaves one of its premises unstated?
hints: The term comes from Greek and is used of everyday arguments that skip an obvious step.
It begins with “enthy-”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enthymeme: an argument with a suppressed premise, such as “Mira is a qualified pilot, so she holds a pilot's licence”.

questions.onCorrect: An enthymeme is an argument that leaves a premise unstated, as your friend's remark about eating early and Mira's licence both do.

misconceptions.feedback: A syllogism has both premises stated. The name you want is for an argument that leaves one out.

questions.prompt: Read: “Water expands when it freezes, so a full, sealed glass bottle left in the freezer will crack; and a cracked bottle leaks, so the freezer will need cleaning.” How many conclusions, intermediate and final, does it draw?
hints: Each “so” introduces a conclusion.
A conclusion can be used again as a premise for a later step.
Count every claim that follows a “so”.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two. The bottle will crack (concluded from the water expanding), and the freezer will need cleaning (concluded from the crack and the leak).

questions.onCorrect: The bottle will crack, and the freezer will need cleaning. The first is a conclusion that then serves as a premise for the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the last claim. The earlier “so” also draws a conclusion.
Check what follows each “so”. The water expanding is a reason that is given, not something concluded.

questions.prompt: Read: “Because all reptiles are cold-blooded and every snake is a reptile, and because cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun, snakes bask in the morning sun.” How many premises does it state?
hints: Find the conclusion first; it is the last clause.
Each “because” introduces reasons. List every separate claim it brings in.
Count the claims offered as reasons, leaving out the conclusion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: all reptiles are cold-blooded; every snake is a reptile; cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Three premises. One “because” clause can hold two claims, and the last clause is the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: That count includes the conclusion at the end. Count only the claims offered as reasons.
The first “because” clause holds two claims joined by “and”, and a second “because” follows it. Count every reason.

questions.prompt: In “We should cancel the picnic, since the forecast says thunderstorms”, which single word signals the premise?
hints: Look for the small word that points at a reason, not at one of the claims themselves.
It sits between the two parts of the sentence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Since” introduces the reason, the forecast. The conclusion is what that reason supports.

questions.onCorrect: “Since” points at the reason, the forecast, so the claim in front of it, that we should cancel, is the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: Those words belong to the claims themselves. Look for the small word that tells you a reason is coming.

questions.prompt: Premises: “If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet” and “The pavement is wet”. Conclusion: “It rained overnight”. Is the argument valid?
hints: Grant both premises. Is there any other way the pavement could have got wet?

acceptedIdeas: No: the pavement could be wet for another reason, such as a burst water main, with both premises true and no rain.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: the pavement could be wet for another reason, such as a burst water main, with both premises true and no rain.

choices.label: No: the first premise might be false.
No: the pavement could be wet for another reason, such as a burst water main, with both premises true and no rain.
Yes: if both premises are true, the conclusion has to be true.

questions.onCorrect: The burst water main is a counterexample, and one counterexample is enough to show an argument invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: The premises leave another way for the pavement to get wet. If a water main burst in the night, both premises would be true and the conclusion false, so the conclusion does not have to follow.

Validity asks whether the conclusion could fail with the premises granted, so whether the first premise is true doesn't decide it. Granting both, the pavement could still be wet from a burst water main, and that makes the argument invalid.

questions.prompt: For the form “p → q, q, so p”, in how many of the four truth-table rows are both premises true?
hints: List the four rows: p and q each true or false.
Cross out every row in which q is false, since the second premise is q.
Check the first premise, p → q, in the rows that remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both premises are true when p and q are both true, and when p is false and q true. In the second of those rows the conclusion is false.

questions.onCorrect: Both premises hold when p and q are both true, and when p is false and q is true. The conclusion is false in the second of those rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every row. The second premise, q, rules some of them out.
Check the row with p false and q true. Is the conditional true there, and is q?

questions.prompt: In “All metals are magnetic; copper is a metal; so copper is magnetic”, which premise is false?
hints: Check each premise against what you know about copper and other metals.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All metals are magnetic.

choices.label: Neither: both premises are true, so the argument is sound.
All metals are magnetic.
Copper is a metal.

questions.onCorrect: The argument is valid and its first premise is false, so it is unsound, which is how a valid argument can reach a false conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: Copper is a metal, so that premise is true. The false one is the claim that all metals are magnetic, since copper, aluminium and gold are not.
The argument is valid, but copper is a metal that is not magnetic, so the first premise is false. That makes the argument unsound, and its conclusion is false as well.

questions.prompt: How many of the eight truth-table rows are counterexamples to “p → q, r → q, so p → r”?
hints: When is the conclusion p → r false?
Fix those values of p and r, and ask which values of q keep both premises true.
Count the rows that survive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The conclusion is false only when p is true and r is false. Then p → q needs q true, and r → q is true because r is false. One row: p true, q true, r false.

questions.onCorrect: The conclusion fails only when p is true and r is false. Then q must be true to keep the first premise true, which leaves a single row.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion fails when p is true and r is false. Check whether both premises can survive in that case.
Fix p true and r false. Only one value of q can then keep the first premise true.

questions.prompt: A valid argument has a false conclusion. What must be the case?
hints: Validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion.
Ask what that leaves for the premises.

acceptedIdeas: At least one premise is false.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At least one premise is false.

choices.label: The argument is not valid after all.
At least one premise is false.
Every premise is false.

questions.onCorrect: If every premise were true, validity would force a true conclusion, so at least one premise is false, though not necessarily all of them.

misconceptions.feedback: One false premise is enough. The others may be true.
The argument is stated to be valid. Ask what validity requires when the conclusion is false.

questions.prompt: A complete truth table for an argument with four different atomic sentences has how many rows?
hints: Two atomic sentences give four rows.
A third sentence can be true or false in each of those rows.
Keep doubling for the fourth.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each atomic sentence doubles the rows: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

questions.onCorrect: Each extra atomic sentence doubles the rows, so four of them give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the table for three atomic sentences. A fourth doubles it again.
That is the number of sentences. Each one doubles the number of rows.

questions.prompt: Dr Okafor argues that a bridge design is unsafe. A councillor replies: “She once lost a contract to that firm, so we can ignore her.” Name the fallacy.
hints: The reply says nothing about the bridge or about her reasons.
Think about what it attacks instead.
Its Latin name means “to the person”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ad hominem: the reply targets the arguer's history instead of her calculations.

questions.onCorrect: The councillor says nothing about her calculations and points instead at something about her, so her argument is never examined.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply does not misstate her view. Look at what it attacks instead.

questions.prompt: Ana: “Speed limits beside schools should drop to 20 mph.” Ben: “Ana wants every car in the country crawling along at 20, which would wreck the economy.” Name Ben's fallacy.
hints: Compare the proposal Ana made with the one Ben criticises.
Ben never mentions Ana herself, only a proposal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straw man: Ben attacks a national limit that Ana never proposed.

questions.onCorrect: Ben attacks a national speed limit that Ana never proposed, so her actual proposal about school zones is left untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: Ben does not attack Ana herself. Compare her proposal with the one he criticises.

questions.prompt: “A feather is light. Whatever is light is not dark. So a feather is not dark.” Name the fallacy.
hints: Both premises are true if you read each one sensibly.
Ask whether “light” means the same thing in each of them.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equivocation: “light” means “not heavy” in one premise and “pale” in the other.

questions.onCorrect: In the first premise “light” means not heavy and in the second it means pale, so the argument equivocates.

misconceptions.feedback: The slip is inside the words. Check whether “light” keeps one meaning throughout.

questions.prompt: Someone says: “Smoking causes cancer, so you shouldn't smoke.” Which added premise gives the most charitable reconstruction?
hints: Charity looks for a premise a thoughtful speaker would accept.
Which options are false, and which claim far more than the speaker needs?

acceptedIdeas: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease.

choices.label: Anything that causes something bad should be banned.
You should avoid what greatly raises your risk of a serious disease.
Everyone who smokes gets cancer.

questions.onCorrect: It is plausible and makes the argument valid without claiming more than the step needs. The other two are false or far stronger than the speaker requires.

misconceptions.feedback: That premise is false, so it makes the argument easy to dismiss. Charity looks for one a thoughtful speaker would accept.
That is much stronger than the speaker needs. Charity does not add more than the argument requires.

questions.prompt: “This newspaper never prints falsehoods. We know this because its front page says so, and that statement must be true, since the paper never prints falsehoods.” Name the fallacy.
hints: Trace where the support for the claim comes from.
Does the support depend on the claim it supports?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Begging the question: the conclusion is used to support the premise offered for it.

questions.onCorrect: The claim that the paper never prints falsehoods is used to back the front page's statement, which was meant to back that very claim.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage offers no choice between options. Trace where its support for the claim comes from.

questions.prompt: “Either we close the library or the council goes bankrupt.” The council in fact has several other ways to save money. Name the fallacy.
hints: Count the options the speaker offers, then count the options that exist.
The speaker presents two options as if there were no others.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A false dilemma: two options are presented as the only ones when others exist.

questions.onCorrect: Two options are presented as the only ones when others exist, so the either-or hides the choices that would avoid both outcomes.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing is assumed in a premise here. Count the options offered against those that exist.

questions.prompt: Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket. He concludes “the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket”. In fact Smith gets the job and, unknown to him, has ten coins himself. Which of the three conditions for knowledge does his belief meet?
hints: Take the conditions one at a time: does he believe it, is it true, and did he have good reasons?
Who gets the job, and how many coins does he have?

acceptedIdeas: All three: belief, truth and justification
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All three: belief, truth and justification

choices.label: Belief and justification, but not truth
All three: belief, truth and justification
Belief and truth, but not justification
Only belief

questions.onCorrect: It meets all three, and yet it is hard to say that Smith knows, which is the trouble Gettier's cases make for the analysis.

misconceptions.feedback: The belief is true, because the man who gets the job, Smith himself, does have ten coins in his pocket. So it meets truth as well as belief and justification.
Smith reasoned carefully from strong evidence, the president's word and his own count of Jones's coins, so his belief is justified as well as true.
He reasoned from strong evidence, which makes the belief justified, and the man who gets the job does have ten coins, which makes it true. It meets all three.

questions.prompt: Ana looks at a usually reliable station clock reading 2:15 and believes it is 2:15. It is 2:15, but the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago. On the justified true belief analysis, does Ana know the time? Answer yes or no.
hints: The question asks what the analysis says, not what you would say.
Check the three conditions mechanically.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes on the justified true belief analysis, since the belief is true, held and justified. Most people judge that she does not know, which is the problem for the analysis.

questions.onCorrect: On the analysis she does, because her belief is held, true and justified. Most people judge that she doesn't, which is the problem.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what intuition says. The question asks what the analysis says, so check its three conditions mechanically.

questions.prompt: Gettier cases show that justified true belief is not ___ for knowledge. Fill the gap with “necessary” or “sufficient”.
hints: Gettier's subjects meet all three conditions.
Which word says that meeting the conditions is not enough?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sufficient: all three conditions hold in a Gettier case, yet the subject does not know.

questions.onCorrect: All three conditions hold in a Gettier case and knowledge is still missing, so they are not enough on their own.

misconceptions.feedback: Gettier did not dispute that each condition is needed. Ask whether having all three guarantees knowledge.

questions.prompt: Henry drives through a county full of barn facades and looks at the only real barn. Could his true belief “that is a barn” easily have been false?
hints: Think about what he would have believed had he looked at one of the facades instead.

acceptedIdeas: Yes: had he looked at any of the facades nearby, he would have formed the same belief and been wrong.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes: had he looked at any of the facades nearby, he would have formed the same belief and been wrong.

choices.label: Yes: had he looked at any of the facades nearby, he would have formed the same belief and been wrong.
No: he is looking at a real barn, so his belief could not have been false.
No: his eyesight is good, so his belief is safe.

questions.onCorrect: Because his belief could easily have been false, it is not safe, and the safety condition says he does not know, which matches most people's verdict on the case.

misconceptions.feedback: His belief is true, but safety asks whether it could easily have been false. Had his eyes fallen on any of the facades around him, he would have believed “that is a barn” just as firmly and been wrong.
Good eyesight is no help in that county, because the facades look exactly like barns from the road. He would have believed the same of any facade, so his belief could easily have been false.

questions.prompt: The no-false-lemmas reply says Smith's reasoning in the coins case passed through a false belief. Which one?
hints: Find the step in his reasoning that did not match what happened.
Which of his beliefs about Jones turned out wrong?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Jones will get the job.

choices.label: Jones will get the job.
Jones has ten coins in his pocket.
The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.

questions.onCorrect: Smith reasoned from “Jones will get the job”, which is false. The other two claims are true.

misconceptions.feedback: He did count ten coins in Jones's pocket, so that claim is true. Find the step in his reasoning that did not match what happened.
That is the conclusion he drew, and it is true. Find the step in his reasoning that did not match what happened.

questions.prompt: Who published the three-page paper “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?” in 1963?
hints: The cases that trouble the analysis bear his name.
His first name is Edmund.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Edmund Gettier, in the journal Analysis, 1963.

questions.onCorrect: Edmund Gettier published it in the journal Analysis in 1963, and his name now labels the kind of case it describes.

misconceptions.feedback: Those philosophers are associated with other cases or with the analysis itself. The 1963 paper is by the author whose name the cases bear.

questions.prompt: Premises: “If I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived by a demon” and “I do not know I am not deceived by a demon”. Conclusion: “I do not know I have hands”. Is the argument valid?
hints: Grant both premises for a moment. Could you then still know that you have hands?

acceptedIdeas: Yes: if both premises are true, the conclusion has to be true.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes: if both premises are true, the conclusion has to be true.

choices.label: No: the first premise is plainly false.
No: the conclusion is absurd, so the reasoning must have gone wrong.
Yes: if both premises are true, the conclusion has to be true.

questions.onCorrect: Because the argument is valid, anyone who rejects its conclusion has to reject one of its premises.

misconceptions.feedback: Whether a premise is false is a question about soundness. Granting both premises, you could not know you have hands, so the argument is valid, and a reply has to reject a premise.
An absurd-looking conclusion is a reason to doubt a premise, but it doesn't show that the reasoning is faulty. Grant both premises and the conclusion cannot fail, so the argument is valid.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher answered the sceptic in a 1939 lecture by holding up his hands and arguing from “here is one hand” to the existence of an external world?
hints: He was a Cambridge philosopher known for defending common sense.
His name is also on the argument you have just compared with the sceptic's.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: G. E. Moore, in “Proof of an External World”.

questions.onCorrect: G. E. Moore gave this answer in his 1939 lecture “Proof of an External World”.

misconceptions.feedback: That philosopher belongs to another part of the story. The 1939 reply with raised hands came from a Cambridge champion of common sense.

questions.prompt: For the form “p → q, ¬q, so ¬p”, in how many of the four truth-table rows are both premises true?
hints: The second premise, ¬q, needs q false. Which rows does that leave?
Check p → q in each remaining row.
Count the rows in which both premises hold.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the row with p false and q false. There ¬p is true, so the form has no counterexample.

questions.onCorrect: Only the row in which p and q are both false keeps both premises true, and in it ¬p is true, so the form has no counterexample.

misconceptions.feedback: The premise ¬q rules out the rows where q is true. Check which of the rest keep p → q true.
¬q removes every row where q is true. Count only what remains.

questions.prompt: Dretske and Nozick hold that you know you have hands but cannot know you are not a handless brain in a vat. Which principle about knowledge must they reject?
hints: It is the principle behind the sceptic's first premise.
It says that knowledge is carried across a known entailment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Closure: the principle that knowledge carries over to what you know your knowledge entails.

questions.onCorrect: Knowing you have hands without knowing you are not a handless brain in a vat means knowledge has failed to carry across an entailment, which is what closure denies.

misconceptions.feedback: Think of a principle linking what you know to what it entails, not a rule of logic.

questions.prompt: Which belief does Descartes' all-powerful deceiver put in doubt that the dream argument leaves standing?
hints: Dreams already put beliefs about the world in doubt.
Ask what would stay true even inside a dream.

acceptedIdeas: Simple truths of arithmetic, such as two and three making five
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Simple truths of arithmetic, such as two and three making five

choices.label: Beliefs about distant cities
Memories of the day before
Simple truths of arithmetic, such as two and three making five

questions.onCorrect: Descartes notes that two and three make five whether he wakes or sleeps, so only a deceiver of unlimited power could make him err even there.

misconceptions.feedback: Dreams already put such beliefs in doubt. Ask what would stay true even inside a dream.
Dreams already put such beliefs in doubt. Ask what would stay true even inside a dream.

questions.prompt: In the Second Meditation, what did Descartes take to survive even the deceiver's deception? Answer in two words.
hints: To be deceived at all, he must be something.
Two words, beginning with “I”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “I exist”: whatever deception he suffers, he must exist to be deceived.

questions.onCorrect: However much the deceiver misleads him, there has to be someone being misled, so “I exist” survives.

misconceptions.feedback: A deceiver could fake all of that. Ask what Descartes must be in order to be deceived.

questions.prompt: 1,000 people are screened. 10% have the condition. The test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 10% of people who do not. Roughly what share of the people who test positive have the condition?
hints: Count the true positives among the 100 with the condition and the false alarms among the 900 without it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About half

choices.label: About 90%, the test's hit rate
About 10%, the share who have the condition
About half

questions.onCorrect: The test finds 90 of the 100 with the condition and raises 90 false alarms among the 900 without it, so half of the 180 positives have it.

misconceptions.feedback: The 90% hit rate is a fact about the 100 people with the condition. The 900 without it produce 90 false alarms, as many as the 90 true positives.
A positive result does raise the chance above the starting 10%. Of the 180 positives, 90 come from the 100 people with the condition.

questions.prompt: The same test, positive for 90% of people with the condition and for 10% of people without it, is used on 1,000 people of whom 1% have the condition. How many people test positive in total?
hints: 1% of 1,000 is 10 people with the condition.
Work out 90% of 10 and 10% of 990.
Add the two results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 have the condition and 9 of them test positive. 990 do not and 99 of them test positive. 9 + 99 = 108.

questions.onCorrect: Nine of the ten with the condition test positive, and so do 99 of the 990 without it, which makes 108.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the people with the condition whom the test catches. Add the healthy people it flags.
That counts only the false alarms. Add the people with the condition whom the test catches.

questions.prompt: A test is positive for 80% of people with a condition and for 5% of people without it. By what factor does a positive result multiply the odds that someone has the condition?
hints: Compare how likely a positive result is with the condition and without it.
Divide one rate by the other.
The hit rate goes on top.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The likelihood ratio is 0.8 ÷ 0.05 = 16, so the posterior odds are sixteen times the prior odds.

questions.onCorrect: The likelihood ratio is 0.8 ÷ 0.05 = 16, so a positive result multiplies the odds by sixteen.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between the two rates. The likelihood ratio compares them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Of 1,000 people, 10% have a condition. A test catches 80% of those who have it and is positive for 5% of people without it. What percentage of the positives have the condition?
hints: Count the true positives: 80% of 100.
Count the false positives: 5% of 900.
Divide the true positives by all the positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 have the condition and 80 of them test positive. 5% of the 900 without it is 45. 80 ÷ (80 + 45) = 80 ÷ 125 = 64%.

questions.onCorrect: There are 80 true positives and 45 false ones, so 80 of the 125 positives have the condition: 64%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of true positives. Express it as a share of all the positives.
That is the number of false alarms. Divide the true positives by all the positives.

questions.prompt: P(H) = 0.2, P(E | H) = 0.5 and P(E | not-H) = 0.25. Find P(H | E), as a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Work out the probability of H together with E: P(H) × P(E | H).
Do the same for not-H, whose probability is 1 − 0.2.
Divide the first result by the sum of the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The joint probability of E and H is 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1, and of E without H it is 0.8 × 0.25 = 0.2. So P(H | E) = 0.1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.2) = 1/3.

questions.onCorrect: E arrives with H at 0.1 and without H at 0.2, so H accounts for one third of the ways E can happen.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P(E | H), the hit rate. Weigh it by how likely H was, then compare it with the other route to E.
That is the joint probability of E and H. Divide it by the probability of E overall.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the error of judging P(H | E) from P(E | H) while ignoring how common H was to begin with? Two words are enough.
hints: The neglected quantity is how common the hypothesis was before the evidence.
It is the number the prior is built from.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Base-rate neglect, also called the base-rate fallacy.

questions.onCorrect: The error is ignoring the base rate: how common the hypothesis was before the evidence arrived.

misconceptions.feedback: Those describe the test. The neglected quantity is how common the condition was to begin with.

questions.prompt: “Lois believes Superman can fly. Lois does not believe Clark Kent can fly. So Superman is not Clark Kent.” The premises are true in the story and the conclusion is false. Is the argument valid?
hints: A valid argument cannot have true premises and a false conclusion.

acceptedIdeas: No: its premises are true and its conclusion false, which no valid argument allows.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No: its premises are true and its conclusion false, which no valid argument allows.

choices.label: No: its premises are true and its conclusion false, which no valid argument allows.
Yes: what Lois believes settles who is who.
Yes: the premises are true, so the conclusion follows.

questions.onCorrect: Descartes' argument from doubt has the same shape, so this case is a reason to suspect it of the same fault.

misconceptions.feedback: True premises are not enough for validity. Here the premises are true and the conclusion is false, and a valid argument can never be in that position.
What Lois believes depends on what she knows, and she doesn't know that Clark Kent is Superman. The argument has true premises and a false conclusion, so it is invalid.

questions.prompt: A critic of substance dualism asks how a thought, which has no size or position, could make the muscles of your arm contract. What is this objection called? Answer in one or two words.
hints: It concerns how the mind and the body act on each other.
The word begins with “inter-”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The interaction problem: how two substances with nothing in common could causally affect each other.

questions.onCorrect: The critic asks how two substances with nothing in common could act on each other, which is the interaction problem Elisabeth put to Descartes.

misconceptions.feedback: That names a different issue. The critic asks how two such different substances could act on each other.

questions.prompt: Elisabeth's argument as “p → q, q → r, ¬r, so ¬p” has eight truth-table rows. In how many are all three premises true?
hints: ¬r means r is false. How many of the eight rows is that?
With r false, what does q → r require of q?
Then what does p → q require of p?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ¬r leaves the rows with r false. Then q → r needs q false, and p → q needs p false. One row remains, and ¬p is true in it.

questions.onCorrect: Only the row with p, q and r all false keeps all three premises true, and ¬p is true in it, so the argument is valid.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many rows ¬r keeps. The other two premises remove more.
Check q → r where r is false: it needs q false. Then check p → q.

questions.prompt: A philosopher holds that being in pain simply is having a certain kind of nerve fibre firing in the brain, in the way that lightning simply is an electrical discharge. Which view of the mind is this?
hints: Their view says the mental and the physical are not two things but one.
The name uses the word you met in Leibniz's law.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mind-brain identity theory, also called type physicalism.

questions.onCorrect: Pain is said to be one type of brain state, which is the identity theory that Place and Smart proposed.

misconceptions.feedback: Their view says the mental and the physical are not two things but one.

questions.prompt: Which statement is Leibniz's law, the indiscernibility of identicals?
hints: Leibniz's law starts from identity.
Check which way each statement runs.

acceptedIdeas: If x is identical with y, then x and y share every property.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If x is identical with y, then x and y share every property.

choices.label: If x and y share every property, then x is identical with y.
If x is identical with y, then x and y share every property.
No two distinct things share any property.

questions.onCorrect: Leibniz's law runs from identity to shared properties. The converse, from shared properties to identity, is a different principle.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs from shared properties to identity. Leibniz's law starts from identity.
That is far stronger than Leibniz's law. It says distinct things never share any property.

questions.prompt: Name the view that there is only one kind of substance, the physical, but that mental properties are not physical properties.
hints: It is a form of dualism about properties, not about substances.
Two words.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Property dualism.

questions.onCorrect: Property dualism allows one kind of substance while holding that mental properties differ from physical ones.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for the view that allows one substance yet says mental properties differ.

questions.prompt: A drinks machine sells a can for 20p, takes 10p and 20p coins and starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 10p, then 10p, then 10p. What happens?
hints: Start in the state with nothing owed and follow the table one coin at a time.

acceptedIdeas: One can comes out, and the machine is left with 10p credited.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One can comes out, and the machine is left with 10p credited.

choices.label: Two cans come out.
One can comes out, and the machine is left with 10p credited.
Nothing comes out, because no 20p coin was inserted.
One can comes out, and 10p comes back as change.

questions.onCorrect: The first coin moves the machine to 10p credited, the second brings out a can and returns it to nothing owed, and the third moves it to 10p credited again.

misconceptions.feedback: The machine gives change only when a 20p arrives while 10p is already credited. The third 10p arrives with nothing owed, so it is simply credited.
Two 10p coins complete the 20p price, so the second coin brings out a can. The third then moves the machine to 10p credited.
Three 10p coins make 30p, which pays for one 20p can with 10p over, and the machine keeps that 10p as credit towards the next can.

questions.prompt: A drinks machine sells a can for 20p and takes 10p and 20p coins. It starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 20p, then 10p, then 20p. How many cans come out?
hints: Run the table coin by coin from nothing owed.
A 20p buys a can in either state.
Count the cans from the first and third coins.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 20p buys a can at once. The 10p sets a credit. The next 20p, with 10p credited, buys a can and returns 10p. Two cans.

questions.onCorrect: The first 20p buys a can, the 10p only sets a credit, and the last 20p buys a second can and returns 10p, so two cans come out.

misconceptions.feedback: A 20p with 10p already credited overpays by 10p but still buys a can.
The 10p in the middle only sets a credit. Track the state after each coin.

questions.prompt: A philosopher argues that if silicon-based Martians winced and withdrew from damage just as we do, they would feel pain too, so pain cannot simply be one kind of human brain state. Which thesis about mental kinds is she relying on? Two words.
hints: It says one kind can be realised in many different ways.
The first word is “multiple”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiple realisability.

questions.onCorrect: One mental kind realised in very different physical systems is multiple realisability, the thesis Putnam used against the identity theory.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a theory about mental states. The thesis wanted says one kind can be realised in many ways.

questions.prompt: A defender of strong AI answers Searle: “Of course the man doesn't understand Chinese, any more than one chip in a computer does. Ask instead about the whole set-up, rulebook, papers and all.” Name this reply.
hints: It moves understanding from the man to something larger.
The reply takes its name from what it says understands.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The systems reply.

questions.onCorrect: The systems reply holds that understanding belongs to the whole system and not to the man alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That names the thought experiment or another reply. The one wanted moves understanding from the man to something larger.

questions.prompt: Two machines, one of gears and one of silicon chips, share the same machine table and receive the same coins. Do they end in different functional states? Answer yes or no.
hints: A functional state is fixed by its place in the table.
Does the table mention gears or chips?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Functional states are fixed by the table, which is identical; only the realisers differ.

questions.onCorrect: Functional states are fixed by the table, which is the same for both machines, and only the materials differ.

misconceptions.feedback: A functional state is fixed by its place in the table. Does the table mention gears or chips?

questions.prompt: What conclusion does Searle draw from the Chinese Room?
hints: Searle grants that the room's replies are fluent.
His claim is about what running a program amounts to.

acceptedIdeas: Running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding.

choices.label: Only biological brains can run programs.
No computer can ever behave as if it understands.
Running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding.

questions.onCorrect: Searle grants the behaviour and denies that implementing a program is enough for understanding.

misconceptions.feedback: Searle grants that the room's replies are fluent. His claim is about what running a program amounts to.
He makes no claim about which things can run programs. His claim is about what running one amounts to.

questions.prompt: Reid's brave officer: the officer remembers being flogged as a boy; the old general remembers taking the standard as an officer but has forgotten the flogging. On Locke's direct memory criterion, which asks whether a later stage itself remembers an earlier one, with which of the two earlier stages is the general identical?
hints: Take each earlier stage in turn and ask whether the general remembers its experiences.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the officer

choices.label: Only the boy
Both the boy and the officer
Only the officer
Neither of them

questions.onCorrect: Since the officer remembers the flogging, he is the boy, so the criterion now says the general is the officer, the officer is the boy, and yet the general is not the boy.

misconceptions.feedback: The general has forgotten the flogging, so he has no direct memory of the boy's experiences, and on Locke's criterion he is identical with the officer only.
The general does remember taking the standard as an officer, from the inside, so on Locke's criterion he is the officer. It is the boy he cannot be.
The general has forgotten the flogging, so he has no direct memory of the boy. It is the officer whose experiences he remembers.

questions.prompt: Reid's case yields general = officer and officer = boy, but general ≠ boy. Which logical property of identity does the direct memory criterion violate?
hints: Look at how the three equations chain together.
The property lets you pass along a chain of identities.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Transitivity: if a = b and b = c, then a = c.

questions.onCorrect: Transitivity: if a is b and b is c, then a is c.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at how the three equations chain together. The property lets you pass along a chain.

questions.prompt: Suppose your brain could be divided into three parts, each transplanted into a new body, and all three survivors remember your past equally well. On a psychological continuity criterion with no extra clause, how many future people are continuous with you?
hints: Does each survivor remember your past?
Does it matter which body holds the memories?
Count the survivors who qualify.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three survivors are psychologically continuous with you, so three people satisfy the criterion. Identity is one-one, which is the problem.

questions.onCorrect: All three survivors remember your past equally well, so three people are continuous with you, and identity cannot hold between you and all of them.

misconceptions.feedback: Continuity does not care which body holds the memories. Count every survivor who remembers your past.

questions.prompt: A teleporter destroys your body on Earth and builds an exact replica on Mars that remembers your life. On the bodily criterion of personal identity, do you survive?
hints: The bodily criterion asks only whether the same body carries on.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the replica's body is a new body and yours was destroyed.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the replica's body is a new body and yours was destroyed.

choices.label: No, because the replica's body is a new body and yours was destroyed.
Yes, because the replica remembers your life.
Yes, because the replica's body is an exact copy of yours.

questions.onCorrect: On a psychological criterion the answer would be yes, which is why the teleporter is such a good case for pulling the two criteria apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Memory is what the psychological criteria look to. The bodily criterion asks whether the same body continues, and yours was destroyed on Earth.
An exact copy is still a different body, built from different matter on Mars. The bodily criterion requires the same body to carry on, so on that criterion you do not survive.

questions.prompt: Stage A is a child of 10. B, aged 30, remembers A's experiences; C, aged 50, remembers B's but not A's; D, aged 80, remembers nothing of A's, B's or C's experiences. On the continuity view, which counts overlapping chains of memory, how many of B, C and D are the same person as A?
hints: Trace each link forward from the first stage.
Is B linked to A? Is C linked to B? Is D linked to C?
Follow the chain from A, and stop where a link is missing.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: A–B and B–C are linked, so B and C are joined to A, but nothing links D to C, so D is not.

questions.onCorrect: A–B and B–C are linked, so the chain reaches C, but D remembers nothing of C, so the chain stops there and only B and C count.

misconceptions.feedback: Continuity follows chains, not just direct links. C does not remember A, but it is joined to A through B.
A chain needs every link. D remembers nothing of C, so no chain reaches D.

questions.prompt: In Parfit's branch-line case the scanner copies you to Mars but fails to destroy your body on Earth. Which survivor does the bodily criterion count as you?
hints: The bodily criterion follows the living body.
Which survivor has the original body?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The person on Earth

choices.label: Both of them
The replica on Mars
The person on Earth

questions.onCorrect: Only the person on Earth has your body. The replica has psychological continuity without bodily continuity.

misconceptions.feedback: The replica has your memories but not your body. The bodily criterion follows the body.
Only one of them has your living body. The bodily criterion follows the body.

questions.prompt: Option B gives a 60% chance of 100 welfare units and a 40% chance of 0. What is its expected utility, in welfare units?
hints: Weight each outcome by its probability.
Work out 0.6 × 100 and 0.4 × 0.
Add the two results.
questions.onCorrect: The weighted values are 0.6 × 100 = 60 and 0.4 × 0 = 0, so the expected utility is 60 units, which beats the sure 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the success value. Weight it by its probability.
That is the weight on failure, not the expected value. Weight the success value by its probability.

questions.prompt: A programme gives 20 units of benefit with probability 0.9 and causes 30 units of harm with probability 0.1. What is its expected utility?
hints: Weight the benefit: 0.9 × 20.
Weight the harm as a negative value: 0.1 × (−30).
Add the two results.
questions.onCorrect: The weighted benefit is 18 and the weighted harm is −3, so the programme's expected utility is 15 units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the benefit's weighted value. The harm still has to be subtracted.
Harm counts against the programme. Give it a negative value.

questions.prompt: A runaway trolley will kill seven people on the main track unless you pull a lever sending it onto a side track, where it will kill two. Counting lives only, how many more people survive if you pull?
hints: How many die if you do nothing?
How many die if you pull?
Compare the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Not pulling: seven die. Pulling: two die. 7 − 2 = 5 more survive.

questions.onCorrect: Seven die if you do nothing and two die if you pull, so pulling leaves five more people alive.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deaths if you do nothing. Subtract the deaths if you pull.
That adds the deaths. You are comparing two options, not totalling them.

questions.prompt: A city could save each of a million commuters ten seconds a day by building a road that forces one family out of its home. A utilitarian adds the commuters' small gains together and finds that they outweigh the family's loss. Name the feature of utilitarianism that produces this verdict.
hints: Ask how the commuters' gains are combined.
The word begins with “aggre-”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aggregation: summing welfare across people, so many small losses can outweigh one great harm.

questions.onCorrect: Summing welfare across people lets many small gains outweigh one family's great loss, and that summing is called aggregation, the feature Scanlon's transmitter room puts under pressure.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the theory, but not the feature in question. Ask how the commuters' gains are combined.

questions.prompt: Who wrote that it is “better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied”?
hints: The line defends a distinction between higher and lower pleasures.
The author called the standard the greatest happiness principle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: John Stuart Mill

choices.label: Immanuel Kant
Jeremy Bentham
John Stuart Mill

questions.onCorrect: Mill wrote it in Utilitarianism, defending a distinction between higher and lower pleasures.

misconceptions.feedback: Kant defends duties that do not depend on outcomes. The line comes from a utilitarian.
Bentham counted the quantity of pleasure. Mill added a distinction between higher and lower.

questions.prompt: Policy X gives three people +4, +4 and −5 welfare units. Policy Y gives each of them +2. By how many units does Y's total exceed X's?
hints: Add the three numbers for X, counting −5 as a loss.
Add the three numbers for Y.
Subtract X's total from Y's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: X totals 4 + 4 − 5 = 3. Y totals 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. 6 − 3 = 3 units.

questions.onCorrect: X totals 3 and Y totals 6, so Y's total is 3 units higher.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Y's total. Compare it with X's total.
Y's total is the larger one. Subtract X's from Y's.

questions.prompt: From a footbridge you could push a heavy stranger onto the track, and his body would stop a trolley that will otherwise kill three. Counting lives only, how does pushing him compare with pulling a lever that sends the trolley onto a side track, where it kills one?
hints: Count who dies and who survives in each case.

acceptedIdeas: The two come out the same: two more people survive either way.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two come out the same: two more people survive either way.

choices.label: The two come out the same: two more people survive either way.
Pushing saves fewer lives, since the stranger dies as well as someone on the track.
Pushing saves more lives, since the stranger stops the trolley outright.

questions.onCorrect: Three survive and one dies in each case, so whatever separates the two, the count cannot be it.

misconceptions.feedback: The stranger stops the trolley by dying, so one person dies and three survive, exactly as with the lever.
His body stops the trolley before it reaches the three, and nobody else is on the track, so one person dies in each case.

questions.prompt: Kant's principle that you must never treat a person merely as a means is called the formula of ___. Fill the gap with one word.
hints: It is named after what all persons share.
Not the formula of universal law.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The formula of humanity.

questions.onCorrect: The formula of humanity says to treat persons always as ends and never merely as means.

misconceptions.feedback: That is another formulation. The one about persons is named after what all persons share.

questions.prompt: Kant tests the maxim “I will push to the front of a queue whenever I am in a hurry” by asking whether everyone could act on it. If everyone did, queues would collapse and the maxim would have nothing to work against. Which of Kant's formulas is this test?
hints: The test imagines the maxim adopted by everyone.
It is not the formula about treating persons.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The formula of universal law.

questions.onCorrect: The test asks whether everyone could act on the maxim, which is the formula of universal law.

misconceptions.feedback: That formulation concerns how to treat persons. This test imagines the maxim adopted by everyone.

questions.prompt: A fire crew lights a controlled burn to save a village, knowing it will destroy one farmer's barn, which they would spare if they could. Which doctrine may permit this burn, while forbidding the crew to destroy the barn as their means of saving the village?
hints: Its name counts the effects of a single act.
Two words, the second is “effect”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The doctrine of double effect.

questions.onCorrect: The barn's destruction is foreseen but not intended as a means, which is the case the doctrine of double effect permits.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the doctrine. Its name counts the effects of one act.

questions.prompt: “If you want to be trusted, keep your promises.” What kind of imperative is this, in Kant's terms?
hints: Does it bind you whatever you want?
It begins with “if you want”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hypothetical

choices.label: Categorical
Universal
Hypothetical

questions.onCorrect: It binds only someone who has the stated goal of being trusted, so it is hypothetical. A categorical imperative binds whatever you want.

misconceptions.feedback: A categorical imperative binds whatever you want. This one depends on a goal.
Universal names a formulation, not a kind of imperative.

questions.prompt: In Thomson's loop case the side track rejoins the main line, so only the one person's body stops the trolley. Is that person's death a means or a side effect of saving the five?
hints: Ask whether the plan would still work if he were absent.
If it needs his body, his death is part of how it works.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A means: if the one were not on the loop, the trolley would come round and kill the five.

questions.onCorrect: If the one were not on the loop the trolley would come round and kill the five, so his body is how the plan works.

misconceptions.feedback: Ask whether the plan would still work if he were absent. If it needs his body, his death is part of how it works.

questions.prompt: Aristotle supposes that ten minae of food is too much and two minae too little. What amount, in minae, is the arithmetic mean of the two?
hints: The arithmetic mean is halfway between the two amounts.
Add the two amounts.
Halve the total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (2 + 10) ÷ 2 = 6 minae. Aristotle's point is that the mean relative to us need not be this amount.

questions.onCorrect: Halfway between 2 and 10 is (2 + 10) ÷ 2 = 6 minae, though Aristotle denies that this is the right amount for everyone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the two amounts. The mean lies halfway, so halve it.
That is the gap between the two amounts. The midpoint lies halfway between them.

questions.prompt: Generosity concerns giving money. Its vice of excess is prodigality. Name its vice of deficiency.
hints: It is the fault of giving too little.
Aristotle's translators also call it stinginess.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meanness, also translated stinginess or illiberality.

questions.onCorrect: Giving too little is meanness, the opposite fault to prodigality, and generosity lies between the two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the excess, or belongs to another virtue. Name the fault of giving too little.

questions.prompt: A parent wants a timid child to become brave. On Aristotle's view, will the child get there mainly by being taught what courage is, or by facing small fears again and again? Answer teaching or habit.
hints: Think of how you learn to build or to play an instrument.
The virtues of thought are the ones taught.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By habit: we become brave by doing brave acts.

questions.onCorrect: We become brave by doing brave acts, so character comes mainly from habit and not from instruction.

misconceptions.feedback: Teaching mainly produces virtues of thought. Think of how you learn to build.

questions.prompt: On a scale from 2 to 10 minae of food, a beginner's right amount runs from 3 to 5 minae. How many minae below the arithmetic mean of the scale is the top of the beginner's range?
hints: Find the arithmetic mean of the whole scale first.
The top of the beginner's range is 5.
Subtract the top of the range from the mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The arithmetic mean is (2 + 10) ÷ 2 = 6 minae. The top of the beginner's range is 5, which is 6 − 5 = 1 mina below it.

questions.onCorrect: The scale's midpoint is 6 and the top of the beginner's range is 5, so six is already too much for a beginner, by one mina.
