misconceptions.feedback: Find the midpoint of the scale first. Then subtract the top of the range from it.
The range's top lies below the midpoint, so take it away from the midpoint, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: Ten minae is too much and two too little. For Milo, a champion wrestler, Aristotle says six minae would be:
hints: Six is only the arithmetic midpoint.
Milo has a large body to feed and trains hard.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Too little

choices.label: Exactly right
Too little
Too much

questions.onCorrect: Six would be too little for Milo and too much for a beginner, because the right amount depends on the person.

misconceptions.feedback: Six is only the arithmetic midpoint. Milo needs more than that.
Milo is a champion with a large body to feed. Ask whether six would be generous for him.

questions.prompt: What Greek word, often translated “happiness” or “flourishing”, names the highest human good for Aristotle?
hints: It is often translated flourishing.
It begins with “eu-”, meaning good.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eudaimonia: living well and doing well, an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

questions.onCorrect: Eudaimonia is the highest good, a life of activity in accordance with virtue, usually translated flourishing or happiness.

misconceptions.feedback: That is another Greek term. The one wanted names the highest good, often translated flourishing.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher's picture of the state of nature ends in the famous line that life there would be “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”?
hints: Whose state of nature is a war of every man against every man?
The author argued for a sovereign with great power.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), chapter 13.

questions.onCorrect: Hobbes wrote this in Leviathan, in 1651, describing life with no common power to keep the peace.

misconceptions.feedback: That philosopher belongs to the story, but is not the author of this line. Think of the author of Leviathan.

questions.prompt: Society A pays its three equal-sized groups 10, 40 and 70 income units. If you are equally likely to land in any group, what is your expected income in A?
hints: Each group is equally likely, so each counts equally.
Add the three incomes.
Divide by the number of groups.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (10 + 40 + 70) ÷ 3 = 40 income units.

questions.onCorrect: With equal chances of each group, the expected income is the average: (10 + 40 + 70) ÷ 3 = 40 units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the top group's income. Add all three incomes and divide.
That is the total. Divide by the number of groups.

questions.prompt: Behind the veil you choose between society A (10, 40, 70) and society B (25, 30, 35), three equal groups each. Which society does the maximin rule choose?
hints: Maximin looks only at the lowest income in each society.

acceptedIdeas: B, because its lowest group gets 25 against A's 10.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: B, because its lowest group gets 25 against A's 10.

choices.label: A, because its average income is higher.
B, because its lowest group gets 25 against A's 10.
A, because its top group gets the most.

questions.onCorrect: Here the two rules part company, since the average picks A, at 40 against 30, while maximin picks B for its better worst position.

misconceptions.feedback: The higher average is what the expected-income rule looks at. Maximin looks only at the worst position, 10 in A against 25 in B, and so chooses B.
Maximin takes no notice of the top group. It compares the worst positions, 10 in A and 25 in B, and chooses B.

questions.prompt: In society D, a quarter of people receive 30 income units and three quarters receive 50. What is the average income?
hints: The groups are not equal, so weight each income by its share.
Work out 0.25 × 30 and 0.75 × 50.
Add the two results.
questions.onCorrect: Weighting each income by its share gives 7.5 + 37.5 = 45 units, nearer to 50 than to 30 because most people receive 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average if the groups were equal. Weight each income by its share.
That is the two incomes added. Weight each by its share of the people.

questions.prompt: Locke held that legitimate government rests on the ___ of the governed. Fill the gap with one word.
hints: Think of agreeing to something.
It is the idea that separates Locke's government from one that simply rules by force.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Consent: people leave the state of nature by agreeing to form a political society.

questions.onCorrect: Locke held that people leave the state of nature by agreeing to form a government, so its legitimacy rests on their consent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of Locke's picture, but not what legitimacy rests on. Think of agreeing to something.

questions.prompt: Rawls's difference principle permits social and economic inequalities only when:
hints: It is a condition on inequalities, not a ban on them.
Whose position does it single out?

acceptedIdeas: They work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.

choices.label: Everyone receives exactly the same income.
They work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.
They raise the average income.

questions.onCorrect: Inequalities are allowed only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, and they must attach to positions open to all.

misconceptions.feedback: Raising the average is the utilitarian aim. The difference principle asks about the least advantaged.
Rawls does not require equal incomes. Inequalities are allowed under a condition.

questions.prompt: In a town of 1,000 people, 300 have a condition. A test is positive for 60% of the people who have it and for 5% of the people who do not. How many people in the town test positive in all?
hints: The people who test positive come from two groups: those with the condition and those without.
Work out 60% of 300 and 5% of 700.
Add the two results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60% of 300 is 180 people with the condition who test positive. 5% of the 700 without it is 35 who test positive. 180 + 35 = 215.

questions.onCorrect: The test flags 180 of the 300 who have the condition and 35 of the 700 who do not, and 180 + 35 = 215.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the people with the condition whom the test catches. It also flags some who do not have it.
That counts only the false alarms. Add the people with the condition whom the test catches.

questions.prompt: A condition affects 1 person in 100. Before any test, what is your prior that you have it? Give it as a percentage.
hints: The prior comes before any test.
It is set by how common the condition is.
A percentage is a number out of a hundred.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The prior is how likely the hypothesis was before the evidence. Here that is 1 in 100, or 1%.

questions.onCorrect: The prior is the probability before the evidence, and here it is set by how common the condition is: 1 in 100, or 1%.

misconceptions.feedback: That kind of number describes the test, not the condition. The prior is how likely the hypothesis was before testing.
That is the chance of not having the condition. The prior is the chance of having it.

questions.prompt: Why divide by all the positives, and not only by the ones who have the condition?
hints: Look at who the question is about.
The people the test flags include some who do not have the condition.

acceptedIdeas: The question asks what share of those who test positive have the condition.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The question asks what share of those who test positive have the condition.

choices.label: False alarms do not matter.
The people with the condition are the majority.
The question asks what share of those who test positive have the condition.

questions.onCorrect: The question concerns everyone who tests positive, and that group includes the false alarms as well as the people who have the condition.

misconceptions.feedback: False alarms are part of the positives, and they change the answer.
In this town the people with the condition are a minority. The reason lies in what the question asks.

questions.prompt: A test is positive for 90% of people who have a condition and for 10% of people who do not. Half of 1,000 people have the condition. What percentage of the positives have it?
hints: Half of 1,000 have the condition and half do not.
Work out the positives in each group.
Divide the positives who have the condition by all the positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 have the condition, and 450 of them test positive. 500 do not, and 50 of them test positive. 450 ÷ 500 = 90%.

questions.onCorrect: Of 500 positives, 450 have the condition. When the base rate is one half, the hit rate and the false alarm rate decide the answer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the prior. Count how many with the condition the test catches and how many without it the test flags.
That is the false alarm rate. Divide the positives who have the condition by all the positives.

questions.prompt: A coin-flip game pays £100 on heads and nothing on tails. Played again and again, about how much do you win per play on average, in pounds?
hints: Heads comes up half the time.
Weight each result by how often it comes up.
Add the two weighted results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Heads half the time pays £100, tails half the time pays nothing: 0.5 × 100 = 50.

questions.onCorrect: Heads comes up half the time and pays £100, tails pays nothing, so the average is 0.5 × 100 = £50 per play.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what heads pays, but heads comes up only some of the time.
Tails pays nothing, but heads pays a lot. Weight each by how often it comes up.

questions.prompt: A gamble gives a 50% chance of 10 units and a 50% chance of 20 units. What is its expected utility?
hints: Weight each value by its probability, then add.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 15 units

choices.label: 10 units
15 units
30 units

questions.onCorrect: Half of 10 plus half of 20: each outcome counts in proportion to its probability.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two values without weighting them. Each counts only half the time.
That is only the lower outcome. Expected utility weights both outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why is the harm written as −20?
hints: Think about what the sign shows.
What should a harm do to the weighted total?

acceptedIdeas: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.

choices.label: Harm matters less than benefit.
So that the probabilities add to 1.
A bad outcome subtracts from the total.

questions.onCorrect: The negative sign makes the harm pull the weighted total down, instead of adding to it as a benefit would.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign shows direction, not importance. A harm pulls the total down.
The probabilities already add to 1. The sign is about the value of the outcome.

questions.prompt: Option A gives an 80% chance of 50 units and a 20% chance of −10 units. What is its expected utility?
hints: Weight the good outcome: 0.8 × 50.
Weight the bad outcome as a negative: 0.2 × (−10).
Add the two results.
questions.onCorrect: The weighted gain is 40 and the weighted loss is 2, so the expected utility is 38 units.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the bad outcome. Weight it and add it as a negative.
That adds the harm instead of subtracting it. The value is negative.

questions.prompt: Is the neighbour's reply a reason about the canteen at all? Answer yes or no.
hints: What does the reply say about vegetables on the menu?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. It says something about Jo, not about whether the canteen should serve more vegetables.

questions.onCorrect: The reply is about Jo, not the canteen. A good reply to an argument speaks to its reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: The reply is about Jo. Ask what it would say if someone else made the same suggestion.

questions.prompt: “You can trust the report, because the report says it is trustworthy.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
hints: Compare the claim with the reason given for it.
Would someone who doubted the report accept its own say-so?

acceptedIdeas: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.

choices.label: The report's author is attacked.
Only two options are offered.
The conclusion is assumed in the reason offered.

questions.onCorrect: The reason offered assumes the very thing it was meant to establish, so someone who doubted the report would gain nothing from it.

misconceptions.feedback: No options are being offered here. Look at how the reason relates to the claim.
Nobody is attacked. Compare the claim with the reason given for it.

questions.prompt: Sam says, “We should add a bike lane on Mill Road.” Kit replies, “Sam wants to ban cars from the town.” Why does Kit's reply leave Sam's proposal untouched?
hints: Compare what Sam proposed with what Kit criticises.
Ask whether anyone has proposed what Kit is arguing against.

acceptedIdeas: It attacks a different, more extreme position.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It attacks a different, more extreme position.

choices.label: It is spoken in a rude tone.
It attacks a different, more extreme position.
It gives no reasons at all.

questions.onCorrect: Kit's reply is aimed at a ban on cars, a position Sam never took, so whatever is said against it says nothing about a bike lane.

misconceptions.feedback: Tone is not the fault. Compare what Sam proposed with what Kit criticises.
Kit does give a reason. The reason is aimed at the wrong target.

questions.prompt: Lena argues for longer library hours. Rob replies: “Lena wants the library open all night, every night, which would bankrupt us.” Name Rob's fallacy.
hints: Compare what Lena proposed with what Rob criticises.
Rob does not mention Lena herself.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straw man: Rob attacks an extreme version of Lena's proposal.

questions.onCorrect: Rob attacks an extreme version of Lena's proposal, one that she never made, and leaves her actual proposal standing.

misconceptions.feedback: Rob does not attack Lena herself. Compare her proposal with the one he criticises.

questions.prompt: One thermostat uses a strip of two metals that bends as it warms, and another uses a digital sensor. Both switch the heating on below 18 °C and off above it. Are they both thermostats?
hints: Is a thermostat defined by what it is made of or by what it does?

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because being a thermostat is a matter of what a device does with the temperature.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because being a thermostat is a matter of what a device does with the temperature.

choices.label: Only the digital one, because a thermostat needs electronics.
Neither, because only a person can decide when to heat a room.
Yes, because being a thermostat is a matter of what a device does with the temperature.

questions.onCorrect: What the two share is their job, and a kind defined by its job is what we have just called a functional kind.

misconceptions.feedback: Thermostats made of bending metal strips worked long before digital ones existed. Both switch the heating on and off at the same temperature, and that is what a thermostat does.

A device that reliably switches the heating on and off at a set temperature is doing a thermostat's job, whether or not it understands what it does. Whether such a device could have a mind is a further question, which this lesson comes to.

questions.prompt: In the drinks machine, what does “nothing owed” (S0) mean?
hints: Look at how the table defines each state.
Which answer says what the state does?

acceptedIdeas: The state in which a 10p leads to 10p credited and a 20p buys a can at once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The state in which a 10p leads to 10p credited and a 20p buys a can at once

choices.label: An empty coin tray
A particular metal part inside the machine
The state in which a 10p leads to 10p credited and a 20p buys a can at once

questions.onCorrect: The table never mentions parts. A state is picked out by what it does next, and in this one a 10p moves the machine to 10p credited while a 20p buys a can at once.

misconceptions.feedback: The table never mentions parts. A state is defined by what it does next.
A tray is a part, and its coins are inputs, not a state. The state is defined by what it does with the next input.

questions.prompt: Why does the machine's response to a 10p depend on its state?
hints: Compare what the table says for a 10p in each of the two states.
The table does not mention the particular coin.

acceptedIdeas: The same coin does different things in different states.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same coin does different things in different states.

choices.label: Coins vary from one to the next.
The same coin does different things in different states.
It counts how many cans it has sold.

questions.onCorrect: A 10p in the state nothing owed sets a credit, and the same coin with 10p credited releases a can, so the state decides what the coin does.

misconceptions.feedback: Every 10p is treated alike. Compare what it does in different states.
The table does not track cans sold. It tracks the state the machine is in.

questions.prompt: A drinks machine sells a can for 20p and takes 10p and 20p coins, giving change when it can. It starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 20p, 20p, 10p, 10p. How many cans come out?
hints: Run the table coin by coin from nothing owed.
Each 20p buys a can in the state nothing owed.
What do the two 10p coins do together?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each 20p buys a can at once, and the two 10p coins together buy a third: 3 cans.

questions.onCorrect: Each 20p buys a can at once, and the two 10p coins together make up a third price, so three cans come out.

misconceptions.feedback: The last two coins also make 20p between them. Track the state after each.
The 10p coins buy a can only together. Track the state after each coin.

questions.prompt: Did Tess know that the coin would land heads? Answer yes or no.
hints: Ask what Tess had to go on.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Her guess was right, but she had no reason for it.

questions.onCorrect: A right answer reached by luck is not knowledge. Something more than being right has to be in place.

misconceptions.feedback: A guess can be right without being known. Ask what Tess had to go on.

questions.prompt: A man holds a well-reasoned belief that turns out to be false. Which of the three conditions for knowledge fails?
hints: He believes it, and he reasoned well. Which condition is left?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Truth

choices.label: Justification
Truth
Belief

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge requires the claim to be true, so good reasons cannot make up for a false belief.

misconceptions.feedback: He does believe the claim, so the belief condition is met. The failure lies with the claim itself, which is false.
His belief is well reasoned, so it is justified. However good the reasons, a belief in a false claim cannot be knowledge.

questions.prompt: Why is Ravi's case, in which he sees rain falling, different from Smith's coins case?
hints: Both men have good evidence.
Compare what each man's evidence is about.

acceptedIdeas: His evidence is connected to the fact that makes his belief true.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: His evidence is connected to the fact that makes his belief true.

choices.label: His evidence is connected to the fact that makes his belief true.
His belief is only probable.
His evidence is stronger.

questions.onCorrect: Ravi's evidence is the rain itself, which is the fact that makes his belief true. Smith's evidence was about Jones, and the fact that made his belief true was about Smith.

misconceptions.feedback: Smith's evidence was strong too. Compare what each person's evidence is about.
Seeing the rain makes the belief secure. The difference lies in what the evidence is about.

questions.prompt: A man is certain his lottery ticket will win, though he has nothing to go on. It does win. Which of the three conditions is missing? Answer in one word.
hints: He believes it, and it turns out true.
What did he have to go on?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Justification: his belief is true and held, but he had no good reason for it.

questions.onCorrect: His belief is held and true, but with nothing to go on it is unjustified, and a lucky guess is not knowledge.

misconceptions.feedback: His ticket does win, so his belief is true. Check what he had to go on.
He is certain, so he does believe it. Check what he had to go on.

questions.prompt: Case A: a surgeon could save five patients who need transplants by taking the organs of one healthy visitor. Case B: a doctor has a drug that one patient needs all of and five patients each need a fifth of, and gives it to the five. In which case is a person's body the way the five are saved?
hints: Ask of each case whether the plan would still work if the one person were absent.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The transplant case

choices.label: The transplant case
Neither case
Both cases
The drug case

questions.onCorrect: Take the visitor away and the transplant plan fails, which makes him a means, while the patient who goes without the drug is a side effect of giving it to the five.

misconceptions.feedback: In the drug case the one patient plays no part in saving the five, since giving them the drug would save them even if he were absent.
Only the transplant plan needs a person's body. In the drug case the five are saved by the drug, whether or not the sixth patient exists.
The visitor's organs are what save the five, so that plan works only because of him.

questions.prompt: Which of these uses the stranger as a means?
hints: Ask whether the plan would fail without his body.

acceptedIdeas: Pushing him so that his body stops the trolley
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pushing him so that his body stops the trolley

choices.label: Shouting a warning to him
Pushing him so that his body stops the trolley
Pulling a lever that turns the trolley, so that it hits him

questions.onCorrect: Only the push needs his body. In the other cases the plan would work without him.

misconceptions.feedback: Without him on the side track the plan would work just as well. His death is a side effect there.
A warning treats him as someone to inform. His body plays no part in the plan.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter morally that the plan needs the stranger's body?
hints: The count of lives is the same in both cases.
Ask what the plan treats him as.

acceptedIdeas: It makes him a tool of the plan.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It makes him a tool of the plan.

choices.label: It saves more people.
Heavy people are rarer.
It makes him a tool of the plan.

questions.onCorrect: A plan that needs his body uses him as an instrument for its success, and that is what the formula of humanity forbids.

misconceptions.feedback: The count of lives is the same in both cases. Ask what the plan treats him as.
His weight is only what makes the plan work. Ask what the plan treats him as.

questions.prompt: Maxim: “I will keep a promise only when it suits me.” If everyone acted on it, could promising still work as a practice? Answer yes or no.
hints: Ask whether anyone would rely on a promise that is kept only when convenient.
What would happen to the practice of promising?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. If promises were kept only when convenient, nobody could rely on them.

questions.onCorrect: If promises were kept only when convenient nobody could rely on them, so the practice would collapse, and the maxim fails the test.

misconceptions.feedback: Ask whether anyone would rely on a promise that is kept only when convenient.

questions.prompt: Does your friend's belief show that Sam and the mayor are different people? Answer yes or no.
hints: Her belief is about what she thinks, not about Sam.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. What she believes about the two names does not change who they pick out.

questions.onCorrect: No. A difference in what she believes is a fact about her, not about Sam or the mayor.

misconceptions.feedback: She has a view about one name and none about the other. Is that a fact about the man, or about her?

questions.prompt: The Morning Star is the Evening Star: both names pick out the planet Venus. The Morning Star has a rocky surface. Which of these must be true?
hints: Think about what “one planet” means.

acceptedIdeas: The Evening Star has a rocky surface.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Evening Star has a rocky surface.

choices.label: Everyone who thinks the Morning Star is rocky thinks the Evening Star is rocky.
The Morning Star and the Evening Star differ in some property.
The Evening Star has a rocky surface.

questions.onCorrect: There is one planet there, so any fact about the Morning Star is a fact about the Evening Star, because both names pick out Venus.

misconceptions.feedback: If they are one planet, no property can differ between them. Think of what “one planet” means.
Someone may not know the two names pick out one planet, and what they think is a fact about them and not about Venus.

questions.prompt: What does the masked-man case suggest about the doubt argument?
hints: Both arguments have the same shape.
Compare “believed by Lois” with “doubted by me”.

acceptedIdeas: “Being doubted by me” may describe my state of mind and not a property of my body.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Being doubted by me” may describe my state of mind and not a property of my body.

choices.label: That Descartes' conclusion must be false.
“Being doubted by me” may describe my state of mind and not a property of my body.
Nothing, because the two cases are unrelated.

misconceptions.feedback: The case shows a weakness in the argument. It does not settle what is true.
Both arguments have the same shape. Compare “believed by Lois” with “doubted by me”.

questions.prompt: “Ben believes Mark Twain wrote Huckleberry Finn. He does not believe Samuel Clemens wrote it. So Mark Twain is not Samuel Clemens.” Valid or invalid?

questions.prompt: Must Ann be the same person as Cy? Answer yes or no.
hints: Picture all three names pointing at people. How many people are there?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. Ann is Bea and Bea is Cy, so all three are one person.

acceptedIdeas: No, because she cannot remember the 20-year-old's experiences from the inside.

choices.label: Yes, because she has the same body.
Yes, because she has the same name.
No, because she cannot remember the 20-year-old's experiences from the inside.

questions.onCorrect: The memory criterion asks whether the later stage remembers the earlier stage's experiences from the inside, and body and name do not come into it.

misconceptions.feedback: Having the same body settles it on the bodily criterion. Locke's criterion looks at memory, and Anna remembers nothing from 20.
A name is not part of the criterion. Look at what the later stage remembers.

questions.prompt: Why is this a problem for the direct memory criterion?
hints: Look at how the three claims chain together.
Forgetting is not the issue.

acceptedIdeas: Identity should pass along a chain, and the criterion breaks that.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Identity should pass along a chain, and the criterion breaks that.

choices.label: Memories can be false.
Generals forget more than boys.
Identity should pass along a chain, and the criterion breaks that.

questions.onCorrect: If the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, then the general must be the boy, but the criterion says he is not.

misconceptions.feedback: Forgetting is not the issue. Look at how the three claims chain together.
Nothing here depends on false memories. Look at how the three claims chain together.

questions.prompt: Each of four stages remembers only the stage just before it. On the direct memory criterion, with how many earlier stages is the last stage identical?
hints: Direct memory reaches only what the stage itself remembers.
Which earlier stages does the last one remember?
Count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the third stage: it is the only one the last stage remembers directly.

questions.onCorrect: The last stage remembers only the third, so on the direct criterion it is identical with that one stage and with no other.

misconceptions.feedback: The last stage does remember the one before it from the inside. Check each earlier stage separately.
Direct memory reaches only the stage just before. Count what it remembers itself.

questions.prompt: Your body is destroyed and an exact replica that remembers your life is built elsewhere. On a psychological criterion, do you survive? Answer yes or no.
hints: A psychological criterion follows memory and character.
Does the replica have both?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The replica has your memories and character, which is what that criterion follows.

questions.onCorrect: The replica has your memories and character, which is exactly what a psychological criterion follows.

misconceptions.feedback: A psychological criterion follows memory and character, and the replica has both.

questions.prompt: How many separate reasons does Maya give for eating early?
hints: Which sentence is the thing she wants us to do?
The rest of what she says is there to back it up. List those claims one at a time.
Count the claims offered as support, leaving out the one they back.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away. “We should eat early” is what they support.

questions.onCorrect: Two reasons back one claim. Seeing which is which is the first move in judging any argument.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the claim Maya wants us to accept. It is what the reasons support, not one of them.
The second sentence joins two claims with “and”. Each is a separate reason.

questions.prompt: In “The shop must be shut, because the lights are off”, which part is the conclusion?
hints: A conclusion is the claim the reasons are offered for.
“Because” points at one of the two parts.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The shop must be shut.

choices.label: The word “because”.
The lights are off.
The shop must be shut.

questions.onCorrect: The shop's being shut is the claim, and the lights being off is the reason offered for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The lights are the reason offered. A conclusion is the claim that a reason supports.
“Because” is an indicator word. It points at a reason, but it is not a claim at all.

questions.prompt: In the passage “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.” why is “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet” the conclusion?
hints: Think about what the other two statements are for.
The same claim could have come last, introduced by “so”.

acceptedIdeas: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.

choices.label: It comes first in the passage.
It is the shortest sentence.
The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.

questions.onCorrect: What the other claims do for it decides the matter. Position and length have no say.

misconceptions.feedback: Conclusions can come last, as in the “since …” passages. Where a sentence sits never settles it.

questions.prompt: Which unstated premise makes “Mira is a qualified pilot, so she holds a pilot's licence” work as an argument?
hints: Ask what has to be true of pilots in general for Mira's case to carry over.
The missing premise should link the stated reason to the conclusion.

acceptedIdeas: Every qualified pilot holds a pilot's licence.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every qualified pilot holds a pilot's licence.

choices.label: Mira has flown many hours.
Every qualified pilot holds a pilot's licence.
Some people who hold a pilot's licence are qualified pilots.

questions.onCorrect: That premise carries the stated reason, that Mira is a qualified pilot, across to the conclusion. Without it the step is a leap.

misconceptions.feedback: That may be true of Mira, but it does not connect being a qualified pilot with holding a licence.
That starts from people who hold a licence, while the argument starts from a pilot. It says nothing about Mira's licence.

questions.prompt: If the friend's two claims are true, must the conclusion be true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Try to imagine both claims being true while the conclusion fails.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The conclusion follows from the two claims, whether or not they are true.

questions.onCorrect: The shape guarantees the conclusion. Whether the claims are true is a separate question.

misconceptions.feedback: Try it. Suppose you know the shop is open, and you do not know it is unburned. Can both hold?

questions.prompt: Which rule of inference takes “p → q” and “p” to “q”? Answer with its Latin name.
hints: It is the rule that affirms.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Modus ponens.

questions.onCorrect: Modus ponens takes a conditional and its first part to its second part, and Moore runs the shared premise this way.

questions.prompt: Why can Moore's argument and the sceptic's both be valid?
hints: Compare where each argument starts.

acceptedIdeas: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.

choices.label: Validity is a matter of opinion.
One of them must be invalid.
They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.

questions.onCorrect: Each argument is valid, and they begin from opposite second premises, so the dispute is about which of those premises to accept.

misconceptions.feedback: Both have valid forms. Compare where each one starts.
Validity is settled by the shape of the argument. The disagreement is about which premise to accept.

questions.prompt: “If I know I have hands, I know I am not a handless brain in a vat. I know I have hands. So I know I am not a handless brain in a vat.” Valid or invalid?
hints: Suppose both premises were true. Could the conclusion still be false?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid: it has the form p → q, p, so q.

questions.onCorrect: It has the form p → q, p, so q, and no row makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

questions.prompt: You must split 12 sweets into three piles, and you will be handed whichever pile turns out smallest. How many sweets should the smallest pile hold, to give yourself the most?
hints: Whatever you make larger, you also make something else smaller.
What happens to the smallest pile if one pile is bigger than the rest?
Which split makes the smallest pile as big as it can be?

questions.onCorrect: Equal piles of four give the smallest pile the largest size it can have, since any unequal split leaves some pile smaller than four.

questions.prompt: Why would people in Hobbes's state of nature accept a sovereign?

acceptedIdeas: To escape a war of all against all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To escape a war of all against all

choices.label: To escape a war of all against all
Because a law of nature already forbids harm
Because the sovereign is kind

questions.onCorrect: Without a sovereign, fear and competition lead to conflict. Obedience is the way out.

questions.prompt: Behind the veil, what do you know?

acceptedIdeas: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours

choices.label: How society is arranged, but not which position is yours
Your own talents
Your own income

questions.onCorrect: You can compare arrangements, but you cannot tilt them towards your own position.

questions.prompt: Why is there no dilemma between society A (10, 40, 70) and society C (20, 45, 95)?

Then compare the lowest income of each.

acceptedIdeas: C does better on the average and for the worst-off.
